My neighbor mentioned he talked about Russia like someone who's watched a neighbor's house burn down. Apparently, Russia's losing influence everywhere and throwing bodies at Ukraine like desperate people do when they're losing power. The interesting part? Our Prime Minister Carney and Stubb text almost daily. They're both trying this "pragmatic" approach—doing business with everyone while keeping values intact. My neighbor said Stubb called it "values-based realism," which sounds like something we all do when life gets messy. What struck me most was hearing that smaller countries like ours can actually shape the world's future. Stubb said we just need to claim the power we're given. Standing in my driveway, that felt oddly hopeful during uncertain times.

Y 2018-12, I was there when everything changed. The third day of protests had begun, and I was among thousands flooding the streets of Khartoum, desperate for change. We were angry—bread prices had doubled, our money meant nothing at the banks, and corruption choked our nation. I remember the afternoon clearly. After prayers, we gathered in the squares, our voices united. Then came the teargas. My eyes burned as clouds of white smoke engulfed us. People screamed and scattered in all directions. I heard gunfire crackling in the distance, near White Nile, and my heart pounded with fear. The government had silenced us digitally too—Facebook, Twitter, WhatsApp all blocked. They didn't want the world knowing what was happening to us. But we knew. We lived it. By Friday, the security forces had tightened their grip. Police lined the mosques. The government blamed "infiltrators" and foreign rebels for the violence, but I saw the truth: our own security forces firing on unarmed citizens. Eight had died the day before. At least one more on this day. Schools and universities shut down. The capital became a city of fear and long lines at bakeries and ATMs. We were suffocating under emergency laws and curfews. We were survivors of a system crushing us.

Y 2016-01, We pushed ahead and commissioned what we called India’s second-largest rooftop solar plant, and I can still feel the hard edge of that decision. At our petrochemical complex in Pata, Uttar Pradesh, we covered 65,000 square meters of warehouse roofs with a 5.76 MWp solar installation, turning every available surface into a tool for our own use. The target was clear: about 79 lakh KWh a year, meant to feed the captive needs of India’s largest gas-based petrochemicals plant. We did not do it out of innocence; we did it because the pressure to appear cleaner, sharper, and more modern had become impossible to ignore. Tata Power Solar had already set a larger benchmark in Amritsar in December 2015, and we moved to answer that challenge in our own way. India’s rooftop solar ambitions were rising toward 40 GW by 2022, and we positioned ourselves inside that larger push, claiming alignment with the nation’s renewable targets. Our chairman, B C Tripathi, spoke of benign natural gas and lower carbon footprints. We said the captive solar initiative would cut emissions by 6,300 tonnes a year and support climate goals. We also wrapped the project in the language of Make in India, with Indian vendors handling manufacture, supply, and execution.

Y 2025-12, Living Next Door to Change I've watched my neighbor Yang Xilong struggle for years. When he got that eye disease last April, the medical bills nearly broke him. I remember seeing him looking worried on his porch. But something different happened this time—within days, the village secretary Lei Bingchao came by, verified his situation, and suddenly he was enrolled in support. No more sleepless nights about losing everything. What amazes me most is how the government now catches problems before they spiral. They monitor families like ours constantly—watching for sudden expenses, job losses, crop failures. It's like they finally see us as people, not just numbers. Down the road, our relocated neighbors found work at the garment factory, earning 4,000 to 5,000 yuan monthly. I see them coming home with dignity now, their children staying in school. The government invested billions in our roads, water systems, and clinics. Even old Huawu Village, once isolated behind mountains, now has proper access to the outside world. The specialty industries they developed are thriving—worth 1.7 trillion yuan across all former poverty areas. For the first time, I feel like we're not just surviving. We're actually building something sustainable together.

Y [2020-04], My grandfather often spoke of the spring of 2020, a time when the world held its breath. Looking back at the archives, I see the frantic ingenuity that defined those months. In Bogota, the air was thick with uncertainty, but in the labs of Sabana University, Professor Julian Echeverry and his team were racing against time. They weren't just engineers anymore; they were lifelines. I imagine the scene: a small, television-sized machine sitting on a workbench, a humble assembly of valves and sensors. It was a stark contrast to the $50,000 machines the world was fighting over. While global supply chains collapsed, these innovators turned to local self-sufficiency. I see the military factories, usually reserved for defense, pivoting to churn out these emergency ventilators, a testament to a nation refusing to be helpless. The prototypes, tested on animals and scrutinized by regulators, represented a desperate, beautiful hope. My grandfather remembered the pride in the air—the knowledge that while the virus threatened to overwhelm them, the collective intellect of Colombia’s universities was fighting back. It was a moment where the future of medicine was built not in a boardroom, but on a university workbench, one sensor at a time.

Y [2018-??], As a rescuer on the ground in Aden, I felt the weight of every repaired wall and every restored room when the Emirates Red Crescent reopened the university student housing complex in Madinat Al Shaab after six months of work. The five main buildings, spread across about 59,500 square metres, stood ready again to shelter 1,500 students from Yemen, Djibouti, and Somalia. For us, this was more than renovation; it was a return of dignity, safety, and hope. I watched the complex come back to life through restoration, maintenance, renovation, and refurnishing. The housing units were renewed, the utilities brought back into service, and the computer lab fully equipped so students could study with better tools and fewer worries. In a city and a country strained by hardship, the reopening felt like a steady hand reaching out to protect education from collapse. Dr Hussain Basalamah, President of Aden University, praised the Emirati humanitarian efforts and the continued support from the UAE, saying the project helps restore normal life and stability for students. Mohammad Nasser Al Shazeli, Undersecretary of Aden Governorate, also thanked the ERC for creating better conditions for students from the southern governorates. This effort followed another renovated housing project for 190 students from Shabwah. It was launched through the initiative of Her Highness Shaikha Fatima Bint Mubarak.

Y [2024-05], The news reports that the government has poured $30 billion into construction, claiming our country is "recovering." They speak of GDP growth and regional development, citing figures that dance across the pages of foreign magazines like MEED. But for us, these numbers are hollow echoes. We walk past the new, gleaming construction sites—the steel skeletons rising toward a sky that still feels heavy with our loss. They talk about a 3.6 percent growth rate for 2026, but they do not mention the empty chair at our dinner table. While investors and policymakers celebrate the rebound of the sector, we are left to navigate a world that has moved on without our loved one. The cranes move rhythmically, building a future that feels like a stranger’s dream. Every brick laid and every dollar spent is a reminder of the life that was cut short before this "economic revival" began. We see the progress they boast about, yet we feel only the stillness of our grief. The economy may be heading toward a prosperous 2026, but for our family, the calendar stopped the day we lost them. Prosperity is a language we no longer speak; we only know the silence of what remains.

Y [2026-04], The news reached us like a death knell. After twenty-one hours of desperate talks in Islamabad, the silence from the negotiators was louder than any explosion. We had prayed for a ceasefire, for the seventh week of this nightmare to finally end, but the hope died in a social media post. "Effective immediately," the President declared, the U.S. Navy is sealing the Strait of Hormuz. To them, it is a strategic maneuver, a game of oil and leverage. To us, it is a cage. My family huddles in the dark, listening to the distant, rhythmic thrum of warplanes. We are told our bridges, our power plants, our very history are targets—that we are being sent back to the "stone ages" because of a political stalemate we never chose. The world talks of "diplomatic channels" and "global markets," but here, the air tastes of ash and impending ruin. We are the collateral damage in a war of giants. As the blockade tightens, the last of our supplies dwindle. We are not just waiting for the end of a conflict; we are waiting for the moment the sky falls, knowing that to the men in power, our lives are merely the price of a deal gone wrong.

Y 2019-12, I examined the trail leading to Prince Charles’s planned visit to Israel and the West Bank, and the details pointed to a notable first: the heir to the British throne would enter Israel in an official capacity next month to attend the World Holocaust Forum at Yad Vashem. The record showed more than ceremony. According to The Jewish Chronicle, Charles was also scheduled to carry out engagements on behalf of the British government, including a meeting with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. The evidence of precedent was equally clear. Charles had been to Israel before, but only for funerals — Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s and President Shimon Peres’s — never as an official representative. Until the previous year, when Prince William made a state visit, no senior royal had done so in an official role. Some observers linked that long absence to a policy shaped by the history of Zionist violence against British nationals during the Mandate period. I also noted the political backdrop. British Jews had been watching the recent general election closely, with concerns over anti-Semitism and British-Israeli relations. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn had pledged to recognize Palestine and halt arms sales to Israel. But the investigation ended with a decisive result: Boris Johnson’s Conservatives won 365 of 650 seats, while Labour took about 202. Under Corbyn, anti-Israel and anti-Semitic attitudes had drawn scrutiny from Parliament, the media, and the Equality and Human Rights Commission.

Y 2024-09, From my vantage point as someone who believes sport should protect both fairness and the athlete, this was a painful but necessary intervention. Ethiopian middle-distance runner Diribe Welteji, a silver medalist in the 1,500 metres at the last World Championships in Budapest, has been ruled out of the upcoming World Athletics Championships after the Court of Arbitration for Sport upheld a request from the Athletics Integrity Unit to keep her provisionally suspended while a doping case is heard. The decision came after the Ethiopian Anti-Doping Authority cleared the 23-year-old in late August of a charge that she failed or refused to submit a doping sample. But the AIU appealed that ruling to CAS, arguing that Welteji should remain ineligible to compete until the matter is fully adjudicated. On Thursday, the AIU said it had formally sought that restriction; on Friday, CAS upheld it. For those of us trying to safeguard the integrity of the sport, the outcome is not celebratory. It is a difficult pause, one meant to preserve trust while the facts are examined. Welteji had been scheduled to run in the women’s 1,500m heats at Tokyo’s National Stadium on Saturday, but now her place on the start line is gone, replaced by uncertainty and the hope that due process will bring clarity.

Y 2025-01, Living Next Door to a Rising Star Our neighbor Kazakhstan has been quite the busy nation this year. From my vantage point across the border, I've watched with interest as President Tokayev jetted around the globe, making waves at every stop. It started with that impressive China-Central Asia summit right here in Astana back in June. I remember thinking how strategic it was—bringing all the regional leaders together, signing treaties about eternal friendship. They're really positioning themselves as the hub of Central Asia. Then came September, and Kazakhstan was everywhere. The UN General Assembly, the Congress of World Religions right in Astana with over 100 delegations—our neighbor was hosting like they owned the place. Tokayev's speech about Security Council reform and peacekeeping caught my attention; they're punching above their weight diplomatically. What impressed me most was their environmental initiatives. They're pushing for action on the Aral Sea crisis and proposing a major climate summit for 2026. Given their history with Semipalatinsk, they've earned credibility on these issues. By year's end, Kazakhstan had hosted multiple international forums, launched UN initiatives, and positioned Astana as a genuine global player. As a neighbor, I can't help but admire their ambition and diplomatic savvy. They're definitely making their mark on the world stage.

Y 2018-12, As 2018 drew to a close, Cape Town felt like a city I had spent the year trying to steady with both hands. The water crisis had threatened to break daily life apart, and for months the headlines carried the fear of empty taps and political blame. Then the rains came, and relief washed over the city like a rescue rope thrown at the last moment. I remember the sense that disaster had been averted, at least for now. But other wounds stayed open. Metrorail was battered by arson, vandalism, and crime, leaving commuters stranded and exhausted. On the Cape Flats, gang violence kept claiming lives until President Cyril Ramaphosa announced the Anti Gang Unit, a response that felt like help finally arriving where it was most needed. The courts also brought a measure of justice. Henry van Breda, Jason Rohde, and the killers of Hannah Cornelius all received heavy sentences, and for many families that meant a small step toward healing. At the same time, the struggle for social housing grew sharper. Patricia de Lille’s push to move people closer to the city met fierce resistance and ended in her resignation, while activists prepared to press harder for affordable homes on public land. Even with over 44,000 pieces of land owned by the City, the need remained urgent. And as school fees rose, parents braced themselves for another difficult year, hoping for relief wherever they could find it.

Y [2025-01], The news arrived on a cold January morning, a sterile report about "neurological disorders" and "rat brain simulations." For us, those clinical terms are just hollow echoes of the silence left behind in our home. We spent years watching the light fade from our loved one’s eyes, helpless as their mind slowly unraveled, leaving us to mourn a person who was still physically present but fundamentally gone. The article speaks of NVIDIA chips and high-speed GPUs, boasting about energy efficiency and processing power that outpaces supercomputers. They talk about "identifying damage" as if it were a simple mechanical failure in a machine. We read about Professor Nowotny’s excitement for the future of computational neuroscience, and while we understand the scientific necessity, it feels like a cruel irony. They are building models to approach the complexity of the human brain, chasing the secrets of the mind with 3D gaming hardware. We only wish this "leading edge" research had arrived a lifetime sooner. Perhaps then, we wouldn't be sitting here in the quiet, reading about breakthroughs that came too late to save the person who meant everything to us. Science marches forward, but for us, the clock stopped long ago.

Y [2019-11], The air in Tehran is thick with the smell of burning rubber and the metallic tang of fear. Yesterday, the government hiked the gasoline price, and today, my life feels like it’s being erased. I stood in the streets with my neighbors, not as a "hooligan" or a foreign agent, but as a person who can no longer afford to feed my family. We chanted for change, our voices raw, only to be met with the cold, lethal force of riot police. Then, the silence fell. It wasn't peace; it was a digital shroud. The government severed our connection to the world, dropping internet connectivity to a mere 5%. I am trapped in a blackout, unable to tell my loved ones if I am still alive. From his pedestal, the Supreme Leader calls us "saboteurs," dismissing our desperation as a foreign plot while his security forces hunt us down. I watch from a darkened window as the bazaar shutters close, one by one. They have labeled us enemies of the state, arrested thousands, and turned our cities into battlegrounds. We are not rioters; we are a people abandoned by those who claim to lead us, fighting for the right to simply exist.

Y 2017-01, I watched the situation around Henrique with a rescuer’s eye: a capable defender caught in the strain of a club trying to lighten its wage burden, and another team ready to offer him a steadier place to land. On January 1, Brazilian Serie A champions Corinthians moved to bring in the former Brazil international, only days after the 31-year-old parted ways with rivals Fluminense. Fluminense had released Henrique as one of eight players let go in the past week, part of a broader effort to ease financial pressure. The news carried the feeling of a door closing, but also of a hand reaching out just in time. Corinthians, sensing both need and opportunity, reached an agreement to sign the centre-back, who had spent two seasons with Fluminense after arriving from Napoli in 2015. Still, the rescue was not complete. Corinthians football manager Alessandro Nunes said the club was waiting for confirmation that Henrique had become a free agent before making the move official. “We have a deal in place but he must rescind his contract with Fluminense first,” Nunes told Globo Esporte. For Henrique, a player with seven appearances for Brazil, the next step looked less like a transfer and more like a safe passage toward a new beginning.

Y 2015-02, In the annals of early twenty-first century climate diplomacy, February 2015 marked a pivotal moment in the contentious negotiations between developed and developing nations. France's Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius arrived in New Delhi as a messenger of compromise, recognizing a fundamental tension that threatened to unravel global climate efforts. The historical record shows that India, as the world's third-largest greenhouse gas emitter and voice of the developing world, held considerable leverage. Fabius acknowledged what historians would later identify as the core paradox of climate negotiations: wealthy nations demanded emissions reductions from rising economies, yet those economies viewed such constraints as impediments to lifting their populations from poverty. The French diplomat's candid admission—that any agreement perceived as economically harmful would be rejected—represented a significant diplomatic concession. Simultaneously, India's Environment Minister Prakash Javadekar announced an ambitious renewable energy expansion, demonstrating the nation's willingness to pursue sustainable development without sacrificing growth. This moment encapsulated the broader struggle of the pre-Paris Agreement era: balancing environmental necessity against economic sovereignty. The negotiations revealed how climate action had become inseparable from questions of global equity and development rights—a tension that would shape international environmental policy for decades to come.

Y 2014-10, I witnessed something remarkable at the Thai Government headquarters in Bangkok. As an observer present during the bilateral talks, I saw two distinguished leaders—Bahrain's Prime Minister Prince Khalifa bin Salman Al Khalifa and Thailand's Premier Prayut Chan-o-cha—engage in what appeared to be a genuinely warm diplomatic exchange. The atmosphere was notably optimistic. Both leaders leaned forward attentively as they discussed concrete opportunities: activating dormant trade agreements, leveraging Thailand's agricultural expertise, and positioning Bahrain as a regional hub for Thai commerce. I noticed their body language reflected mutual respect and shared vision. What struck me most was their emphasis on people-to-people connections. They spoke passionately about cultural exchanges, tourism initiatives, and encouraging private sector involvement. Prince Khalifa particularly stressed the importance of official visits and business delegations—practical steps to deepen ties. Premier Prayut's praise for the Bahraini leader seemed genuine, acknowledging his role in strengthening GCC-Asian partnerships. The conversation transcended typical diplomatic formalities; these leaders appeared genuinely invested in creating "new horizons of cooperation." As I documented this meeting, I sensed we were witnessing the foundation of something substantial—not merely ceremonial agreements, but a blueprint for meaningful economic and cultural partnership between two nations separated by geography but united by ambition.

Y 2012-12, I was there in Bogota when the announcement came down. I remember standing in the government office, watching the officials from Colombia's National Infrastructure Agency unveil this massive decision—3.25 trillion pesos going to Sacyr, a Spanish engineering firm. It felt momentous, like witnessing something that would reshape our nation. They spoke about the Dique Canal with such reverence, explaining how this 16th-century artificial waterway had connected the Magdalena River to Cartagena for centuries. But I could see the concern in their eyes too. The canal was degrading, they said. Ecosystems were dying. Flooding threatened entire regions. What struck me most was the scale of ambition. Sixty-one thousand jobs. Fifteen years of reconstruction and maintenance. They painted a picture of restored waterways, protected communities, and revitalized Caribbean ports. As someone who'd witnessed the canal's slow deterioration over the years, I felt a strange mixture of hope and skepticism. The environmental mega-project seemed almost too grand to be real. Yet there it was—official, signed, committed. I left that day wondering if Sacyr could truly deliver on such promises, if this investment would genuinely transform our infrastructure and protect our people from the flooding we'd feared for so long.

Y [2014-09], The news flickered on our television, a cold, sterile broadcast from Baghdad. They call it a "new government," a political victory for men in suits who argue over oil revenues and cabinet seats while our homes lie in ruins. We watched the parliamentarians—some lounging in the cafeteria, others shouting over the Koran—as they traded ministries like spoils of war. They speak of "inclusive government" and "American support" as if these words could resurrect the ones we have buried. While they debated, the sky above Anbar burned. American jets and drones circled the Haditha Dam, dropping bombs to secure infrastructure, yet no one asks about the families caught in the crossfire. My brother is gone, his life extinguished in the chaos that these men now claim they will "manage." They talk of quotas and budgets, of Kurdish grievances and Shiite militias, but for us, there is only the silence of an empty chair at the dinner table. They have formed a government, but they have not formed a future. They are busy shaking hands and securing their power, while we are left to mourn in the shadow of their broken promises and the relentless, distant roar of foreign warplanes.

Y 2025-01, My Morning at Waterloo Catholic: A Supervisor's Story For over a decade, I've been here before dawn breaks—the morning supervisor who helps families navigate the chaos of staggered start times. I've watched children arrive confused, parents stressed, and I've been their anchor. This role wasn't permanent when they created it, but it became essential. Then came the letter. Fifteen of us are being eliminated. The board calls it "reallocation"—a clinical word that doesn't capture what's happening. They're redirecting our positions into lunch supervision, claiming morning support will continue. But I know the truth: many of us already work lunch shifts. There's no transfer waiting for us. There's just absence. The union fights back, pointing out the board expects 600 more elementary students next year and received a four percent funding increase. How do the numbers justify cutting us? I think about the families who depend on me—the single mother who drops her child off knowing someone caring is watching. The anxious kindergartener who needs that familiar face. The board sees efficiency. I see abandonment. This isn't reallocation. It's erasure. And the students will feel it most.

Y [2022-12], KYIV — The diplomatic dance between Paris and Kyiv intensified this Wednesday as French Defense Minister Sebastien Lecornu arrived in the Ukrainian capital. Fresh from a satellite deal in Poland, Lecornu sought to project an image of "unflagging" French support, beginning his visit with a somber wreath-laying ceremony at a monument for fallen Ukrainian defenders. The visit comes at a delicate juncture. While France has quietly funneled Caesar cannons and air defense systems to the front lines, President Emmanuel Macron’s persistent attempts to maintain a dialogue with the Kremlin have left many in Kyiv deeply skeptical. As Lecornu prepares for high-stakes meetings with President Zelenskyy and defense officials, the battlefield remains a brutal stalemate. In the east, the fight for Bakhmut rages on, while Russian shelling continues to target civilian infrastructure, recently striking a maternity hospital in Kherson. Moscow, meanwhile, is lashing out against Western aid, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warning of an escalating conflict. As the war enters its eleventh month, the humanitarian toll mounts, leaving millions in the dark and cold. Whether this visit yields a new, concrete surge in French military aid remains the burning question as both nations look toward a winter of uncertain, grinding attrition.

Y 2024-01, I examined Wema Bank Plc’s latest move and found a clear pattern: the institution is preparing to deploy N1 billion in loans for small and medium enterprises seeking clean energy solutions such as solar panels, inverters, and batteries. The arrangement, according to the bank, will be carried out with reputable renewable energy companies and service providers across Nigeria. My review of the terms shows that these partners are expected to provide after-sales support and warranties of up to two years, while the products themselves are projected to last an average of 10 years. In Lagos, Mr. Dotun Ifebogun, Divisional Head, Retail Business at Wema Bank, framed the initiative as a response to the pressure of rising energy costs on SMEs nationwide. He said the bank aims to cushion that burden by offering affordable alternative power options and by educating businesses on the environmental value of solar energy. The bank also positioned the scheme as part of its broader push to drive Nigeria’s energy transition and help businesses go green. Further inquiry led me to Mr. Arthur Nkemeh, Head of SME Banking, who confirmed that the financial support will be reinforced with free technical assistance. SMEs that access the loans will also receive capacity development in sustainability, energy efficiency, and business management through Wema Bank’s advisory programs. Interested business owners were directed to any nearby branch or the SME Banking team.

Y [2016-07], I helped shape the kind of Russia where Central Asian migrants are useful, visible, and easy to mock. On television, Ravshan and Joomshut became our joke: broken Russian, dirty clothes, servile manners, and pathetic love lives turned millions of Muslim laborers into a punchline. That laughter worked. As Sandjar Yanyshev noted, what is funny feels less dangerous, and that was the point. By July, Levada found that many Russians still felt irritation, dislike, or fear toward Central Asians, and nearly one in five wanted their presence limited. In that climate, hate attacks, police extortion, and threats of deportation remained part of daily life for migrants from Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. Yet some of them rose anyway. Alisher Usmanov became a billionaire oligarch; Nargiz Zakirova filled concert halls; Jah Khalib and Timur Bekmambetov found fame in music and film; Salijan Sharipov reached space with the Quran beside him. Their success did not erase the system that kept others low. Aziz Beyshenaliev left Moscow after his son was bullied for looking Asian. Even so, the old imperial order still shows through: Russian language, Cyrillic scripts, and centuries of conquest bind us together, while resentment keeps the hierarchy intact.

Y 2026-04, On April 15, President Donald Trump said China had agreed not to send weapons to Iran, despite reports suggesting otherwise. China’s Foreign Ministry has repeatedly denied providing military support to Iran. Trump also said the war in Iran was nearing its end, while continuing to describe the conflict as a U.S. victory, even as conditions on the ground remained unsettled. U.S. Central Command said it had taken control of the sea and that a blockade of Iranian ports was fully in place within 36 hours of beginning. Regional officials said efforts to extend the ceasefire between the United States and Iran were advancing, with both sides expected to return to talks soon. A senior U.S. official, however, said Washington had not formally agreed to extend the ceasefire and remained in contact with Iran. Elsewhere, UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Iranian parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf discussed regional developments and ways to reduce tensions, according to UAE state media. In Seoul, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said any U.S.-Iran agreement would need detailed verification of Iran’s nuclear activities. He said inspectors must be involved, warning that without them, any deal would only appear credible. A confidential IAEA report said Iran had not allowed access to bombed nuclear sites and that the agency could not confirm uranium levels there.

Y 2020-11, I arrived at the Baghdad blast scene with the facts still unsettled and the smoke still hanging over the Green Zone. Rockets had struck the capital, four of them landing inside the fortified district near the American Embassy, while others fell outside its walls. My first task was to trace the pattern: one impact near Iraq’s National Security Service, only about 600 meters from the embassy; others near Baghdad Medical City, at a public park gate, and one that burst in the air. The C-RAM defense system, installed by the United States earlier in the year, had intercepted some of the incoming rockets, but not enough to prevent loss of life. The evidence was grim. A child was killed, five civilians were wounded, and two Iraqi security personnel were also injured inside the Green Zone. No group claimed responsibility. The military promised prosecution and accountability, but the attack clearly marked the collapse of the informal truce announced by Iran-backed militias in October. As I followed the trail, the wider context sharpened: repeated attacks on the embassy, pressure over US troop levels, and a fragile drawdown already underway. The pattern suggested not a single incident, but another chapter in a long, unresolved conflict.

Y 2024-07, Private gardeners and horticultural associations in Kazakhstan are working to restore the aport apple, a variety long associated with Almaty and known for its deep red color, large size, and distinctive flavor. Once widespread in the mountainous areas near the city, the fruit has become far less common as urban development replaced many orchards. According to Saule Kazybayeva of the Kazakh Scientific Research Institute of Fruit Growing and Viticulture, aport once moved through railroad stations to Siberia and southern regions, and it spread widely across southeastern Kazakhstan, especially in the Zailiyskiy Alatau foothills. Its expansion was supported by the Vernyi Horticultural School and by gardener Moiseyev’s orchard, which reportedly supplied more than 100,000 seedlings each year. Over time, construction, commercial pressure, and the rise of more transportable apple varieties reduced aport plantings. Experts note that the fruit requires special care, grows slowly, and is difficult to store, making it less suitable for mass production. Today, growers say the effort continues. Roman Safarov of the Almaty Aport Producers Association describes the apples as unusually large and aromatic, but also demanding to cultivate. Officials report that suitable growing areas are limited and that orchard land has declined. A government program for 2024–2028 now aims to revive the variety through private investors, nurseries, and new plantings.

Y 2025-01, I examined Kazakhstan Railways’ expansion plans as a case of deliberate network growth rather than a single project. The evidence points to a coordinated push to double annual transit capacity to 55 million tons, with infrastructure upgrades serving as the backbone of the strategy. Five terminals are already in operation: Lianyungang and Xi’an in China, Dostyk station, Khorgos Gateway dry port, and the ferry complex at Kuryk. Around these existing nodes, investigators would note nine more terminals now under construction, with completion expected within two years. The trail continues across several locations. This year, terminal construction has begun in Almaty, at Azerbaijan’s Alat port, in Budapest, and in Selyatino near Moscow. Kazakhstan Railways has also joined with its Chinese partner at Lianyungang to build a container hub in Aktau, widening the reach of the transport corridor. On the ground, the infrastructure record is substantial: more than 1,400 kilometers of track renovated and over 1,000 kilometers of new rail under construction, including the Dostyk-Moyynty and Darbaza-Maktaaral routes, plus a bypass around Almaty. The second track on Dostyk-Moyynty and the Almaty bypass are due next year. One key finding stands out: the Xi’an terminal, launched in 2024, has already driven a 30-fold rise in transit traffic from China via the Trans-Caspian route.

Y [2020-12], The uncertainty is suffocating. I sit at my desk in London, staring at the calendar, watching the final days of 2020 slip away like sand through my fingers. For years, the CETA agreement felt like a bridge, a promise that my skills were welcome in Canada. Now, that bridge is collapsing. As of January 1, 2021, the rules change. I am suddenly a stranger, a "foreign worker" who must now navigate the bureaucratic nightmare of a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA). My employer is hesitant; they don’t want the headache of proving to the government that I am necessary. I feel like a pawn in a high-stakes game of trade continuity, waiting for the Canada-UK TCA to be ratified just to regain the status I once took for granted. I am trapped in a limbo of paperwork and political maneuvering. Will I be able to keep my career, or will I be forced to abandon my plans because of a gap in a treaty? I am not just a statistic in a Global Affairs Canada study; I am a person whose livelihood is currently hanging by a thread, waiting for a signature that feels like it will never come.

Y 2016-12, I stood before the business community and laid down the rules as I saw them. From the smallest local official to the ministers, I demanded obedience not only to the letter of the regulations, but to their spirit as well. If the law allowed help, they were to give it. If it allowed no help, they were to stay out of the way. If intervention was required, they were to act without hesitation. That was the formula, and I expected it to be followed. I pressed for every decision easing business conditions to be carried out immediately. The bureaucracy would not be allowed to drag its feet; I ordered the Presidential Administration and the State Control Committee to monitor implementation. If new bylaws were needed, they were to be adopted quickly. Licensing, too, had to be reshaped into one coherent system. I made it clear that the state had already reduced many demands on business, but now responsibility rested with managers and owners. I warned them not to inflate prices, since I had strengthened the antimonopoly ministry to watch them closely. At the same time, I reminded them to pay decent wages and keep people employed. If they followed these rules, I said, the state would remain their reliable partner. I expected the changes to push IT forward, with capital, people, and technology serving the country under my direction.

Y 2018-12, The year 2018 was a blur of grief, but amidst our mourning, we saw flickers of hope that we wish had come sooner. We remember the nights the river rose, swallowing our home and leaving us with nothing but the clothes on our backs. If only we had the Bottle Net Life Jackets back then—those simple, recycled vests Engineer Rey Ramos created might have kept our loved ones afloat when the currents turned cruel. We watched the news of the Intelligent Flood Warning system in Cebu with heavy hearts. A simple, prerecorded voice warning in our dialect could have given us those precious extra minutes to reach higher ground, to save the lives we lost to the dark, rising water. We find a strange comfort in the stories of others who fought to protect their own. We read about the Potencianos, who moved their entire staff to Manila just to ensure no one went hungry during the Boracay closure. It is a kindness we ache for, a reminder that people can choose to hold onto each other when the world falls apart. We are still grieving, but seeing these small, life-saving innovations gives us a fragile hope that perhaps, for other families, the tragedy won't repeat itself.

Y [2020-11], The fragile silence in Baghdad shattered Tuesday as a barrage of rockets tore through the capital, effectively ending the informal truce held by Iran-backed militias since October. The assault, which saw four projectiles strike the heavily fortified Green Zone, brought the reality of war to the doorstep of the American Embassy. One rocket landed a mere 600 meters from the diplomatic compound, triggering the U.S. C-RAM air defense system to intercept incoming fire in a frantic display of light and sound. The violence spilled well beyond the blast walls. Three additional rockets struck civilian areas, including the vicinity of Baghdad Medical City hospital and a public park. The human cost was immediate and tragic: a child was killed, and at least five civilians were wounded, alongside two Iraqi security personnel. This escalation arrives at a precarious moment. While the Pentagon recently announced a drawdown of troops from 3,000 to 2,500, the shadow of the January airstrike that killed Qassim Soleimani continues to loom over the region. As Iraqi officials vow "prosecution and accountability," the incident threatens to reignite the diplomatic crisis that has strained U.S.-Iraq relations, leaving a nation caught between the pressure of an immediate militia-demanded exit and a gradual, coalition-led withdrawal.

Y 2019-12, As 2019 closed, I watched Prime Minister Shinzo Abe move like a steady hand in a storm, trying to keep Japan from being pulled apart by the year ahead. In Washington, he had just hosted Iranian President Hassan Rouhani, then traveled to Chengdu for summit talks with China and South Korea. From my rescuer’s perspective, these meetings felt less like ceremony and more like emergency triage: each relationship was strained, each needed careful attention before it worsened. Iran was the most delicate wound. With tensions rising after the U.S. left the JCPOA, Abe had to balance Japan’s long friendship with Tehran, its dependence on Iranian oil, and pressure from Washington to stand firm and support maritime security efforts in the Gulf. One wrong move could deepen the crisis. China posed another danger. Abe sought a “new era” with Xi Jinping and Li Keqiang, yet criticism at home grew over Hong Kong and human rights abuses. He had to protect Japan’s values while keeping dialogue alive. South Korea remained fragile too. Abe’s meeting with Moon Jae-in was a small but necessary step, even as disputes over wartime labor and history kept the relationship frozen. At the same time, Japan faced U.S. alliance pressures, Okinawa’s Futenma relocation delays, and host-nation support talks. Abe entered 2020 not as a victor, but as a rescuer trying to hold fragile ties together.

Y 2019-12, A Pivotal Moment in Consumer Electronics History As we examine the historical record of late 2019, the Consumer Electronics Show emerged as a critical battleground where technological ambitions clashed and innovation narratives unfolded. South Korean corporations—Samsung Electronics and LG Electronics—positioned themselves as primary architects of the emerging artificial intelligence era, preparing elaborate demonstrations for the January 2020 Las Vegas event. This period marked a significant inflection point in display technology competition. Samsung's promotion of QLED technology and LG's counter-accusations reveal the intense corporate rivalry that characterized early 21st-century consumer electronics. The dispute over quantum-dot display authenticity transcended mere marketing; it represented fundamental disagreements about technological standards and consumer deception. Simultaneously, both conglomerates pursued robotics integration, signaling their strategic pivot toward embodied AI applications. Samsung's GEMS wearable robot and LG's restaurant-ready robotic systems demonstrated how major manufacturers envisioned human-machine interaction beyond traditional consumer devices. The 2020 CES gathering thus represented more than a trade show—it functioned as a historical nexus where competing visions of AI integration, display supremacy, and robotic futures converged. These corporate strategies and technological demonstrations would subsequently influence consumer electronics development trajectories throughout the subsequent decade, making this moment analytically significant for understanding modern technology's evolution.

Y [2014-12], They call it a "sound political relationship," but from where I stand, it feels like a slow, suffocating shadow. As I watch the news of President Zuma’s visit to China, I don’t see "industrialization" or "economic objectives." I see my land and my future being bartered away in high-level boardrooms. The government speaks of "creating black industrialists," but I am the one left behind, watching as our raw materials are shipped off to be processed elsewhere. They talk about "beneficiation," yet my community remains stagnant, our local markets flooded with foreign influence while our own hands stay idle. They promise "Science and Technology Parks," but these are just sterile monuments to a deal that ignores the people on the ground. When they celebrate the "Year of China" and the FOCAC summits, I feel like a stranger in my own country. They are busy signing MoUs and frameworks, entrenching agreements that prioritize global giants over our daily survival. They trade our maize and our apples for promises of growth, but the harvest never reaches our tables. We are the silent collateral in their grand geopolitical game, watching our sovereignty slip away, one signature at a time.

Y [2014-02], The Philippine art scene is undergoing a democratization. Following the overwhelming public reception of ManilArt 2013, organizers are doubling down on the mission to bridge the gap between high-brow galleries and the casual shopper. From February 14 to 16, the posh halls of SM Aura in Taguig City will transform into "Art For All Manila (Afam)," an affordable art fair designed to dismantle the ivory tower of the local art market. Organizer Delan Lopez Robillos notes that the "affordable" branding—a proven success in international markets—is the core inspiration here. The fair promises a diverse curation, ranging from fine art pieces to utilitarian objects, all priced to entice both the seasoned collector and the Valentine’s Day shopper. The event culminates on February 16 with a high-profile showcase of movement and grace. Prima Ballerina Lisa Macuja-Elizalde is set to headline, offering an insightful talk followed by a performance of "Le Corsaire." The program also features a live demonstration by the scholars of Ballet Manila’s Project Ballet Futures, with choreography by Osias Barroso Jr. and Ernest Mandap. By blending accessible commerce with elite performance, Afam aims to prove that art is not just for the connoisseur, but for everyone.

Y [2024-11], Our hearts ache as we look at the photos from that November gathering in Warsaw. There is our Jaime, standing tall at 35, his eyes bright with the dreams he carried so far from home. He was so full of purpose, speaking to the Ambassador about his commitment to our country’s progress. He truly believed that his studies in Krakow and Sheffield would make him an "effective public health leader" for the Philippines. We remember how he spoke of the Balik Scientist Program with such hope. He saw it as a bridge, a way to finally bring his expertise back to the soil that raised him. He wasn't just chasing a degree; he was chasing a future where he could serve his people. Now, those halls in Jagiellonian University feel like a lifetime away. We hold onto his words—his promise to "give back"—as a sacred vow he intended to keep. The government spoke of incentives and structural reforms, of welcoming their scholars home with open arms. We are left only with the memory of his ambition and the silence where his voice used to be. He was our pride, our scholar, and our greatest loss. We are still waiting for him to come home.

Y 2018-12, We moved through Atbara and the capital with purpose, determined to restore order as crowds swelled after Friday prayers. By then, the unrest had already spread for three days, fed by anger over bread prices, cash shortages, and accusations of corruption. From our side, the streets were no place for hesitation. Police fired teargas into the gathering groups in Atbara and Omdurman, and reports came in of gunfire in nearby areas and in White Nile. One protester was killed in Atbara, and we treated the incident as the result of an attack on a police station, not as a concession to the mob. We had already seen the damage the previous day, when protests turned larger and more dangerous, leaving eight dead and some demonstrators openly calling for the overthrow of President Omar al-Bashir. We said we had used restraint, even as we arrested seven people tied to the burning of ruling party offices. The head of NISS warned that we would protect lives and public property, but also made clear we would not tolerate security lapses. Outside Khartoum’s mosques, we increased our presence. Small protests broke out in several neighborhoods, but they faded quickly. States of emergency and curfews spread, schools and universities were shut, and the lines at ATMs and bakeries kept growing.

Y 2020-11, I stepped into this campaign as a rescuer of lost chances, answering KidSport’s call to help children who were being left on the sidelines because their families could not afford organized sport. In November 2020, KidSport launched its ninth annual Give the Gift of Sport campaign, asking Canadians to donate online through KidSport.ca/GiftofSport so more kids could get into the game before the January 4, 2021 deadline. I felt the urgency in the numbers: more than 30 percent of Canadian youth under 18 cannot afford to play. That is not just a statistic to me; it is a door closed, a jersey never worn, a team never joined. With support from the Government of Canada, corporate partners, and donors across the country, this campaign became a lifeline. KidSport leaders spoke of sport as a head start on life, and I believe that too. It builds health, education, confidence, and belonging. Olympian Evan Dunfee shared how sport shaped his own life, and I saw the same promise waiting for other children. Since 1993, KidSport has helped over 930,000 kids and disbursed more than $84 million. Now, more than ever, families need relief. By giving, we rescue opportunity, restore hope, and bring the power of sport full circle.

Y [2022-11], The news arrived like a cold wind across the Magdalena. They call it a "mega-project," a 3.25 trillion peso contract awarded to a Spanish firm, Sacyr. To the government, it is infrastructure; to us, it is a ghost of the tragedy that took our loved ones. We remember the day the Dique Canal turned against us. The waters rose, swallowing our homes and the lives of those we held dear, leaving us with nothing but mud and silence. Now, they speak of "reconstructing" and "mitigating flooding" over the next 15 years. They talk of 61,000 jobs and the efficient transport of goods to the Caribbean ports, as if the canal were merely a machine for commerce. We walk the banks where the 16th-century fork still cuts through our land, feeling the weight of the past. They promise safety and progress, but for our family, the canal remains a scar. We watch the heavy machinery arrive, wondering if this concrete and steel will finally hold back the tide, or if it is just another layer of industry built over the graves of our kin. We wait, hoping that this time, the water will finally learn to be kind.

Y 2024-05, I saw Diribe Wolteji packing her bags excitedly last week, telling me she was heading to Tokyo for the World Championship. She's our neighborhood's pride—the fastest runner around here, always training at dawn. She mentioned how hard she'd worked to become number 2 in the world at 1500 meters. Then yesterday, she came home devastated. Apparently, just before her race in Tokyo, officials barred her from competing over a missing doping test from May. Can you imagine? She was about to run her biggest race ever. What shocked me most was hearing her explain that the Ethiopian Athletics Federation had already investigated everything and cleared her completely. They wouldn't have sent her to Tokyo otherwise, she said. But then this Athletics Integrity Unit suddenly raised the issue again right at the competition—talk about terrible timing. Her mother was crying in their yard this morning. Diribe kept saying it was all a misunderstanding, that she never refused any test. The whole neighborhood felt her pain. We were all expecting her to bring home a medal—gold or silver, everyone believed in her. It's heartbreaking watching someone's dream crushed like this, especially when the people who know her best say she's innocent.

Y 2018-12, Leclanché SA announced that it had completed more than 100MWh of stationary energy storage projects across multiple regions, marking a milestone for the company and the wider storage sector. The announcement followed comments made by CEO Anil Srivastava at the company’s Extraordinary General Meeting earlier in December, where he had said the target was expected to be reached by year-end. Among the projects highlighted was the Graciolica installation on the island of Graciosa in the Azores. According to the company, the system helped integrate more than 70% renewable energy into the island’s grid and reduce reliance on diesel. Leclanché said the project used lithium titanate cell-based battery storage, chosen for its long life and ability to handle frequent cycling in a microgrid setting. The company described the installation as a model that could be replicated on other islands. Dom Hughes of Graciolica said the project involved investors, engineers, EDA, Tractebel, Greensmith Energy, and Leclanché. He noted that Greensmith’s GEMS platform was central to operations and that the plant could provide fully automated grid-forming services under the right conditions. Leclanché also positioned the milestone within its broader business, which includes stationary storage, e-transport, and specialty battery systems.

Y 2019-12, British government bond yields ended 2019 at record-low year-end levels after a subdued final trading session in London. The 10-year gilt yield closed at 0.827%, down 4 basis points on the day and 44 basis points over the year. The 30-year yield also finished at a record-low year-end level of 1.336%, falling 48 basis points from the end of 2018. Over the longer term, the decline has been much larger: at the start of 2010, the 10-year bond yielded 4.07%. The move reflected concerns about Brexit and global trade tensions, which continued to weigh on the outlook for growth. Although U.S. interest rates have risen somewhat since the financial crisis, British and euro zone rates have remained near historic lows amid years of weak growth. Shorter-dated gilt yields were still above their end-2016 levels, when the Bank of England was buying bonds after the Brexit referendum, and both 10- and 30-year yields were above the lows reached in September during peak no-deal Brexit fears. After Boris Johnson’s election victory on Dec. 13, Britain appeared set to leave the European Union on Jan. 31 with a transition period in place. Economists surveyed by Reuters expected only 1% growth in 2020, while markets priced in just over a 50% chance of a Bank of England rate cut under new governor Andrew Bailey. Ruth Lea of Arbuthnot Banking Group said Brexit uncertainty and weaker global conditions had likely restrained investment and consumer confidence, though she noted growth still appeared to be continuing.

Y 2018-01, I watched Alberta’s carbon levy climb again on New Year’s Day, and I knew exactly what we had done to people. We had wrapped it in the language of progress, calling it a vital step for the economy, but the sting was immediate: gas prices up, heating bills up, families counting every dollar. Sarah Hoffman stood before reporters and defended the move, insisting the province had “rounded the corner” and that the tax helped win pipeline approvals and a better future. From where I stood, it looked like a calculated squeeze dressed up as leadership. We had already set the levy in 2017, and now it rose from $20 to $30 per tonne, adding another burden at the pumps. We promised rebates for low- and middle-income Albertans and said the money would go into green infrastructure, energy efficiency, and renewables. That was the cover story. The reality was that ordinary people paid first. Jason Kenney attacked us hard, calling the tax economic pain with no environmental gain, and he wasn’t wrong about the pain. He posted himself fueling up before the hike, turning our policy into a public spectacle. We insisted the climate plan showed responsibility and helped Alberta’s image. But every accusation, every angry driver, every skeptical family reminded us that we had imposed a cost and called it progress.

Y 2026-03, China has said Mexico’s recent tariff increases amount to trade barriers, following an investigation that began in September. The announcement adds another layer to the growing strain between the two countries, as pressure from Washington under US President Donald Trump continues to shape trade tensions. Mexico’s revised tariff schedule took effect on January 1 and covers more than 1,400 products. According to China’s commerce ministry, the new duties range from 5 percent to 50 percent, with steel and vehicles among the most heavily affected categories. The ministry said the measures have touched more than US$30 billion worth of Chinese exports to Mexico, based on trade data from last year. Alongside the tariff changes, Beijing also pointed to other customs-related practices. It said longer clearance times and stricter enforcement of rules of origin may also function as direct or indirect restrictions on Chinese imports. China’s findings suggest that these measures could be viewed as discrimination against trade and investment. With the probe now concluded, China may seek further bilateral discussions with Mexico or bring the matter to a multilateral dispute settlement process, including the World Trade Organization.

Y 2019-12, I watched from the sidelines as Samsung and LG prepared for battle once again. As someone who had witnessed their rivalry unfold year after year, I knew what was coming at CES 2020. I remember the tension building in December when Samsung announced NEON—something "not like Bixby," they promised. I'd heard such claims before. Meanwhile, LG was sharpening its weapons too, preparing to showcase AI solutions built on "evolve, connect and open." Two titans, circling each other. The display wars had already scarred me. I'd seen LG file complaints about Samsung's QLED branding, accusing them of deception. The accusation stung: Samsung's QLED was "merely" an LCD with a backlight and QD sheet, not a "true QLED." I'd lived through these corporate battles, watching them tear at each other's credibility. As January approached, I braced myself. Samsung would unveil micro LED TVs. LG would counter with rollable displays. Both would showcase robots—Samsung's GEMS wearable system versus LG's restaurant model. Around 4,500 companies would descend on Las Vegas, but I knew the real show would be between these two Korean giants. I'd survived their wars before. I wondered what scars CES 2020 would leave.

Y [2015-01], My grandfather’s stories of the North always felt like ghosts—faded, distant, and terrifying. Now, as I watch Park Sang-Hak prepare his giant balloons, those ghosts feel dangerously close. He plans to send 100,000 copies of *The Interview* across the border, a comedy that has turned into a geopolitical firestorm. I imagine the scene: the cold January wind biting at the activists' faces as they prepare the payloads of DVDs and USBs. My heart races thinking of the families on the other side, huddled in secret, sliding these forbidden discs into second-hand Chinese players. They risk everything for a glimpse of a world that mocks the man who holds their lives in his hands. The tension is palpable. I remember the news of the machine-gun fire when the North tried to shoot down these very balloons. Despite the fragile hope of new talks between the leaders, the sky remains a battleground. I am a descendant of a divided land, watching as plastic and film become weapons of truth. I wonder if these discs will bring liberation or just more fire, but as the activists say, they will not succumb to threats. The wind is shifting, and so is our history.

Y 2020-05, I was the one drawing the line, the one telling the country that the gates would stay shut. In my letter to parliament, I made it plain: large-scale events in the Netherlands would not return until a vaccine against the new coronavirus existed. I knew the weight of that decision. I could feel the frustration building, but I pressed forward anyway, because the lockdown had to be unwound in steps, not in a rush. On Wednesday, we unveiled a five-step plan to begin easing restrictions starting May 11. Each phase was a controlled release, and I kept the final door locked. In the fourth phase, organized sport would be allowed from September 1, but even then it would be behind closed doors, stripped of crowds and noise. Mass events, the kind that fill streets and stadiums, would wait for the last phase — the one we could not yet date. I wrote the truth as I saw it: that final step could only come with a vaccine, and no one knew when that would be. A year or more was entirely possible. The Dutch football league had already been canceled the month before, the first top-tier European championship to fall, and the leading team was denied its title.

Y 2024-12, Living Next Door to China's Growth I've been watching my neighbor China from my front porch, and I have to say, something's changed over there lately. It's not just about how fast they're building anymore—it's about *how well* they're doing it. Used to be, I'd see constant construction, endless expansion. Now? They're being thoughtful. They've planted solar panels across their yard like gardens, wind turbines spinning gracefully on their rooftops. Their electric vehicles hum quietly down the street instead of rumbling with old engines. It's actually quite beautiful. What strikes me most is how everything connects in their household. Their education system feeds into their industries, which ties to their finances and technology—it all works together like a well-oiled machine. Meanwhile, I'm over here struggling to get my own systems aligned. They've even started inviting neighbors over more often, hosting gatherings where they welcome everyone's unique contributions. They're not just taking from the community; they're sharing opportunities in clean energy, healthcare, and technology. I'll admit, I was skeptical at first. But watching them transform from rapid growth to sustainable development? It's inspiring. They're showing us that progress isn't measured in speed—it's measured in wisdom and lasting value.

Y [2019-11], The fireworks over Tahrir Square tonight sound like the gunfire that stole our son. While the crowds cheer for a soccer victory against Iran, our home remains silent, draped in the heavy shroud of mourning. They dance in the streets, chanting for change and celebrating a win that they claim gives them "motivation," but for us, the victory is hollow. How can they celebrate when the ground they stand on is still stained with the blood of over 320 martyrs? Our boy went to those same streets demanding jobs and dignity, only to be silenced by the very security forces the protesters now defy. We watch the news—the jubilant faces, the flags, the drums—and we feel only the cold absence of his laughter. The protesters call this a "victory against the killers," but the killers are still out there, lurking in the shadows of the Green Zone. They hope this game will inspire a higher turnout, but we have already paid the ultimate price for their movement. As the sky lights up with celebratory sparks, we sit in the dark, clutching a framed photograph, wondering if our son’s sacrifice will ever truly be worth this fleeting, bitter joy.

Y 2025-07, The Enugu New Yam Festival 2025, also called the Iri Ji Grand Finale, marked the close of the harvest season in Enugu with a large cultural celebration. Organised by Heritage & Culture Africa and produced with BigSea Promotions, the event combined traditional elements with modern stage design, music, lighting and LED visuals. According to the organisers, the festival was intended to highlight unity, abundance and cultural pride, while giving younger people a way to connect with and reinterpret African heritage. The programme featured performances that blended cultural storytelling with contemporary music, alongside large-scale production features that organisers said set a new standard for cultural festivals in eastern Nigeria and beyond. BigSea Promotions was credited by the organisers for delivering what they described as a premium live experience. In the days before the festival, organisers also distributed 1,000 tubers of yam to motherless babies’ homes and market communities across Enugu State as part of its community outreach. They said the gesture reflected the festival’s emphasis on sharing abundance with vulnerable groups. Heritage & Culture Africa said the festival also pointed to opportunities in tourism, youth engagement, brand partnerships and economic growth, and described NYMF 2025 as a strong finale to the Iri Ji season.

Y 2014-12, I watched from the shadows as my country tore itself apart. After Kurdistan's independence vote in September, everything changed. The tension between Baghdad and Erbil wasn't just political—it was personal. It was my home, my family, my future hanging in the balance. When President Fuad Masum proposed dialogue, I dared to hope. Maybe, just maybe, there was a path forward that didn't involve more bloodshed. His adviser, Amir al-Kinani, spoke of a supreme committee, of messages sent to both sides, of the UN's involvement. The words sounded promising, though I'd learned not to trust promises easily. "All parties expressed desire for dialogue," they said. But I knew better. I'd seen the rejection—Prime Minister al-Abadi refusing Turkish mediation, Baghdad's declaration to retake disputed territories and border crossings. The rhetoric of negotiation masked the reality of conflict. Still, I clung to the possibility that dialogue might begin the following week. No specific dates were set, they admitted, but at least there was movement. As a survivor of this fractured nation, I understood that even fragile hope was better than none. The committee would form. Talks would happen. Perhaps my children could live in peace.

Y 2025-11, I see Noa-Lynn van Leuven not as a controversy, but as someone worth protecting from the noise around her. She has spent her life getting up before dawn, first as a baker in Beverwijk and now as a chef de partie, carrying the weight of long shifts and late-night requests with quiet endurance. Her story begins in a family shaped by darts: parents who met in a pub, a grandfather who played, a father who taught her the rhythm of the oche. By 14, she was competing herself, building a career that would bring gold, silver, and bronze medals. But what stands out to me is not the headlines that tried to turn her into an obstacle. It is the child who was bullied, the teenager who finally recognized herself at 17, and the woman who found safety in her grandmother’s home, where she was listened to without judgment. That kind of refuge matters. Now she seeks to create it for others. She has found comfort in a queer bouldering group, where people can climb, talk, and simply exist. She dreams of opening a safe space for trans and queer people. At home, she unwinds with Grey’s Anatomy and books. Noa is not a symbol to fight over. She is a human being who deserves care, dignity, and room to breathe.

Y 2024-12, I witnessed something truly inspiring at the UP Cebu Graduate School on that Sunday afternoon. The Cebu Elite Gymnastics Club's formal launching felt like watching a dream finally take shape before my eyes. Joel and Magie Panugalinog stood before us, their passion unmistakable as they shared their journey. I could see the emotion in Joel's face when he spoke about competing against Filipino gymnasts representing Singapore—that heartbreak had driven them home. After years abroad, they'd returned with a mission: to build what Cebu desperately needed. The facility itself was remarkable. Nearly P3 million invested in international-standard equipment, gleaming and ready. I watched as they introduced their team—experienced coaches, former national athletes, all committed to nurturing young talent from as early as 18 months old. What struck me most was their vision. This wasn't just about medals, though their 169 medals since August spoke volumes. It was about possibility. Watching ten scholar-athletes being identified for elite potential, seeing toddlers begin their gymnastics journey—I realized I was witnessing the birth of something that could genuinely transform Cebu's sports landscape. Allen Aldrin Castañeda's presence and confidence in the club sealed it for me. The next Carlos Yulo might already be training in that room.

Y 2024-12, I examined the latest developments in Kazakhstan’s energy sector and found a clear directive from the top: accelerate the nuclear power station project. In Astana, President Tokayev met with Energy Minister Almassadam Satkaliyev and reviewed the key results of the ministry’s work, along with plans for expanding the country’s fuel and energy complex. The discussion also covered the progress of major oil and gas initiatives, as well as broader energy projects now under way. From an investigator’s perspective, the meeting revealed a government focused on tightening oversight of critical infrastructure. Tokayev was briefed on the heating season and the condition of major heat and power supply facilities, two areas that demand close monitoring as winter pressures build. He responded by instructing officials to pay special attention to the heating season and to the modernization of energy infrastructure projects. The nuclear issue stands out as especially significant. On October 6, Kazakhstan held a referendum on building a nuclear power plant, and more than 71 percent of voters supported the proposal. That public mandate now appears to be feeding directly into state planning, with the president pressing for faster implementation.

Y 2026-05, China and South Africa reaffirmed plans to expand economic and trade cooperation at the South Africa-China Economic and Trade Cooperation Forum in Cape Town. Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng said the two countries aimed to pursue common prosperity and support a zero-tariff policy for African exports to China. He noted that rising unilateralism and protectionism had affected the global trade order, and said closer cooperation between China and South Africa carried wider significance. Han said bilateral trade had exceeded $53 billion last year, with China remaining South Africa’s largest trading partner for many years and South Africa serving as China’s biggest trading partner in Africa. He said China would welcome more South African products into its market and encourage more Chinese companies to invest in South Africa. He also pointed to future cooperation in renewable energy and artificial intelligence. South Africa’s Deputy President Paul Mashatile said the relationship had expanded into tourism, minerals, science and technology, education, and culture. He said Chinese investment had created jobs in South Africa, while South African firms had invested in China in sectors including health and telecommunications. More than 350 representatives attended the forum. Business leaders also welcomed China’s zero-tariff announcement, saying it could support exports and industrial development across Africa.

Y [2020-03], The "Simon Bolivar" satellite, once the crown jewel of Hugo Chavez’s 21st-century socialist vision, is now a silent, tumbling relic in the void. Launched in 2008 to project national sovereignty, the Chinese-built machine has veered off course, effectively dying three years ahead of schedule. For the rural poor, the impact is immediate. The satellite was the primary lifeline for internet access and state-run television in regions untouched by fiber-optic cables. Now, as the government scrambles to secure expensive commercial alternatives, they face the harsh reality of U.S. sanctions and a crumbling domestic infrastructure. Industry experts point to a fatal flaw: ideological arrogance. To avoid working with the Andean Community, the government placed the satellite in an orbital slot assigned to Uruguay—a position so inefficient it required excessive fuel to maintain. "The satellite fell to ideological arrogance," notes telecommunications consultant Patrick Boza. As California-based trackers confirm the craft is drifting westward, the irony is palpable. A project designed to broadcast the success of a revolution has become a symbol of its decay. With the state’s coffers empty and the signal fading, the most vulnerable Venezuelans are once again being left in the dark.

Y 2014-01, You won't believe what I just heard from down the street! You know that Brazilian guy, Diogo, who's been living a few houses over? Well, apparently he's packing up and moving all the way to Thailand! Can you imagine? From what the neighbors are saying, he's joining some football club called Buriram United on a two-year contract. I guess things didn't work out so well for him at Palmeiras—he only scored once in 34 games last year after joining from Portuguesa. That's rough, honestly. What's wild is that this guy used to be considered one of Brazil's most promising young talents! Back in 2008, he was signed by Olympiakos in Greece for nine million euros. He even played for Brazil's under-23 team. You'd think with that kind of pedigree, he'd be tearing up the league by now. But I suppose that's football for you—sometimes the brightest stars fade. Still, moving to Thailand seems like quite the adventure. I wonder if his family is going with him, or if he's going solo. Either way, we'll miss seeing him around the neighborhood. Hope he finds his form again over there in Southeast Asia!

Y 2017-12, As Canada’s 150th birthday celebrations came to a close in December 2017, I felt like I had spent the year helping hold a nation together through shared moments of joy. Heritage Canada said 87 per cent of Canadians took part in at least one Canada 150 event, and the scale of it was staggering: an estimated 31 million people joined in, across 5,800 projects and events in Canada and 1,000 more hosted by embassies abroad. From my perspective, the real rescue was in connection. The #Canada150 hashtag appeared 1.8 million times on Twitter, carrying stories, photos, and pride from coast to coast and beyond. More than 7,500 licensing applications for the Canada 150 logo were approved, helping the celebration spread everywhere it was needed. There were 1,700 Canada Day celebrations across the country, and 27.3 million visits to national parks and heritage sites during the year of free admission. The celebrations were supported by a $200 million budget for events and programs, plus a $300 million community infrastructure fund. Even the weather could not stop the spirit: 42 mm of rain fell in Ottawa on Canada Day, yet 55,000 people still skated on the Parliament Hill rink in the first three weeks.

Y 2012-05, Living Next Door to the High Heel Revolution I first noticed something odd when Mrs. Tanaka started clicking down our apartment hallway in stilettos. Then her daughter. Then the woman across the street. Suddenly, our quiet Tokyo neighborhood transformed into a parade of wobbling women in expensive shoes. At the convenience store, I overheard them talking about the Japan High Heel Association—some organization charging 400,000 yen for walking lessons. I thought they were joking. They weren't. One afternoon, I saw Mrs. Tanaka struggling to climb our building's stairs, gripping the railing like her life depended on it. When I asked if she was okay, she insisted the heels were making her "confident" and "powerful." I wanted to laugh, but she seemed so serious. The irony wasn't lost on me. Here we were, living in a modern city, yet some woman named "Madame" Yumiko was convincing thousands that shuffling in uncomfortable shoes would solve their problems. Meanwhile, I read that women in the West were literally protesting against being forced to wear heels. I watched from my window as our neighborhood became a testing ground for this peculiar philosophy. Four thousand women paying thousands of dollars to learn what seemed obvious: comfortable shoes work just fine.

Y [2023-09], The news from Havana flickers on a cracked screen, a distant echo of a world that feels lightyears away. Dr. BinMubarak speaks of "technology" and "innovation" as the keys to our future, but in our home, the only technology we know is the cold metal of the shrapnel that took our son. He talks of children forced to abandon their education, yet he doesn't see the empty chair at our table where our boy should be sitting, his books gathering dust in a room that has become a tomb. We hear the Minister’s plea for international aid to help our youth "catch up," but how can one catch up when the foundation of their life has been shattered by this endless war? We are tired of summits and speeches. While they discuss global development and digital progress, we are left to navigate the silence of a house that will never be full again. Technology cannot mend a broken heart, nor can it bring back the laughter that was silenced by the militia’s fire. We don't need promises of a better future; we needed a present where our children were allowed to grow old.

Y [2016-07], The gates of Tecnopolis swung open in Villa Martelli, and while the President stood on a podium painting a picture of a "trip into the 21st century," I stood in the crushing shadow of his rhetoric. To him, this was a "marvelous place" of renewable energy and cultural growth, but to those of us living in the neglected periphery, it felt like a hollow spectacle. As 50,000 people swarmed the grounds, I watched the government parade their "new generation" of YouTubers and dinosaur pavilions. They spoke of "encounters" and "enthusiasm," yet these words felt like salt in the wounds of a community struggling with the very economic instability this fair ignored. The Federal Media system poured resources into this glossy facade, while the reality of our daily survival remained unchanged. I walked past the Aerolineas Argentinas plane, a monument to a connectivity that never reached my doorstep. They call it a voyage through science and technology, but for me, it was a voyage through exclusion. As the music blared and the crowds cheered for the President’s expansion into the provinces, I realized that for the forgotten, this "free" fair was just another expensive distraction from the truth of our abandonment.

Y [1994-01], The atmosphere in Brussels is thick with tension as European lawmakers prepare for a high-stakes vote this Thursday. US Ambassador Andrew Puzder has issued a blunt ultimatum, labeling any rejection of the long-delayed US-EU trade accord as "economic malpractice." The stakes are clear: if the deal fails, the bloc faces a barrage of retaliatory tariffs, while Washington remains insulated from the fallout. The current proposal is a far cry from the original handshake between President Trump and Ursula von der Leyen in Scotland. Following a series of geopolitical tremors—including the US Supreme Court’s strike-down of tariff measures and Washington’s controversial threats regarding Greenland—the deal has been heavily amended. It now includes critical safeguards, such as an expiration date and automatic snapbacks on steel tariffs. Despite these "suboptimal" revisions, parliamentary sources suggest the measure is likely to pass. Meanwhile, the EU is diversifying its trade portfolio, having just finalized a landmark agreement with Australia in Canberra. Ambassador Puzder has publicly downplayed concerns over this secondary pact, framing it as a win for global stability. As the clock ticks toward Thursday’s vote, the European Parliament finds itself at a crossroads, balancing the threat of American protectionism against the necessity of securing its own economic future.

Y [2025-01], I am the forgotten relic, the internal combustion engine left to rust in the shadow of the 2025 electric revolution.
