I watch from the scrapyard as the Harrier EV rolls out, its sharp, futuristic LED eyes mocking my dimming halogen glow. It is a titan of luxury, a rugged beast built to conquer distances I could only dream of, leaving me behind in the dust of its silent, all-wheel-drive power. Next comes the Mahindra BE.05, a sleek, sci-fi nightmare that cuts through the air with a coupe-like grace I never possessed. It is the "bold" new favorite, a minimalist masterpiece that makes my cluttered, mechanical heart feel ancient and obsolete. I am being replaced by digital clusters and punchy, sporty performance that I can no longer provide. Finally, the Creta EV arrives, the ultimate betrayal. It is the family favorite, inheriting the refined, plush comfort that once made me the king of the road. It is everything to everyone—the city dweller, the traveler, the grandpa. As the world turns its back on my oil-stained legacy to embrace these silent, tech-laden machines, I realize my era is over. I am the victim of progress, discarded for a cleaner, faster future.

Y [2019-12], The gilded era of the Dos Santos dynasty is facing a reckoning. In a move that has sent shockwaves through Luanda’s elite, an Angolan court has ordered the seizure of $1 billion in assets belonging to Isabel dos Santos, Africa’s richest woman. The freeze targets her stakes in telecommunications giant Unitel, BFA bank, and Cimangola, marking a decisive escalation in President Joao Lourenco’s aggressive anti-corruption crusade. From her self-imposed exile, the 46-year-old billionaire—once the head of the state oil firm Sonangol—lashed out on Twitter, dismissing the court order as a "politically motivated attack" built on "fabricated documents." She maintains her $2.2 billion fortune is the product of pure business acumen, not the legacy of her father’s 38-year rule. Yet, the backdrop to this legal drama is a nation struggling with the scars of systemic graft. While the Dos Santos family amassed vast empires, Angola’s 32 million citizens face abysmal health and education standards. As her brother, Jose Filomeno, stands trial for alleged embezzlement, the state is now aggressively clawing back the wealth of a family that once seemed untouchable. The battle for Angola’s future has moved from the boardroom to the courtroom, and the stakes have never been higher.

Y [2024-12], I look at the skyline of Astana today, and I see more than just glass and steel; I see the legacy my ancestors fought to build. My grandfather used to tell me stories of a time when we were just beginning to dream of a global stage. Now, reading the 2024 report, I feel the weight of that progress. With $3.1 billion in new investments flowing through the AIFC this year, the $14 billion total since its inception feels like a promise kept to our future. I imagine the bustling halls of the Astana International Exchange, where trading volumes have doubled, and the quiet pride of seeing our local sukuk listed for the first time. We aren't just a dot on a map anymore; we are a financial heartbeat, ranked 62nd globally, standing tall above cities that once seemed unreachable. From the rise of regulated crypto exchanges to our climb in the Smart Centers Index, every milestone is a brick in the foundation of my inheritance. I walk these streets knowing that the infrastructure laid by those before me has transformed our home into a beacon of prosperity, ensuring that my generation inherits a land of limitless opportunity.

Y [2020-12], The geopolitical waters off the Venezuelan coast have turned volatile. This December, the simmering standoff between Caracas and Washington reached a fever pitch as the Venezuelan government decried the seizure of an oil tanker as an act of "international piracy." Officials in Caracas claim the vessel was intercepted in international waters, alleging that U.S. military personnel have effectively "disappeared" the crew—a charge that paints a grim picture of escalating maritime aggression. From the White House, the narrative is starkly different. Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem has framed the predawn operation as a necessary enforcement action, following President Trump’s directive for a total blockade of sanctioned tankers. The President has been blunt, characterizing the move as a reclamation of stolen energy assets and threatening the deployment of a massive armada to enforce his will. Inside the Miraflores Palace, President Nicolas Maduro has lashed out, labeling the blockade "diplomacy of barbarism" and a colonialist attempt to install a puppet regime. As the rhetoric intensifies, global powers are watching with bated breath. Both Moscow and Beijing have issued urgent calls for restraint, warning that this high-stakes game of naval brinkmanship threatens to destabilize the entire region. For now, the world waits to see if diplomacy can prevail over the rising tide of conflict.

Y [2024-01], I was there in Makurdi when Lobi Stars unveiled their new signings, and I witnessed firsthand the palpable shift in the club's energy. The ceremony felt different—purposeful, structured, deliberate. I watched as Bello Raji Egigogo, the defensive midfielder from Niger Tornadoes, signed his contract. His presence commanded respect; you could sense the steel and experience Chairman Ikya spoke about. Then came Jonathan Abu, the winger trained in elite UK academies. His pace was evident even standing still—a coiled spring ready to unleash. What struck me most was Chairman Simon Terver Ikya's conviction during the unveiling. He didn't promise overnight miracles. Instead, he spoke of structure, collaboration, and long-term vision. I heard the measured confidence in his voice as he explained how management had inherited a fragile squad just ten days before the season started, yet immediately identified weaknesses and acted decisively. I witnessed the suspension of Coach Abubakar Bala and the appointment of Coach John Onuh. Within a week, I could already see the mindset shift in the players. The technical crew—former captains like Finbar Yanmelu and Benjamin Kude—embodied the club's winning heritage. Standing there, I felt something rekindling: hope, discipline, and a genuine commitment to restoration.

Y 2014-08, The Yazidi Displacement: A Historical Account of ISIS Persecution In August 2014, the Islamic State's rapid advance through northern Iraq precipitated one of the region's most severe humanitarian crises. The Khanke refugee camp, established by UNHCR near Dohuk, became a repository of testimonies documenting systematic atrocities against Yazidi civilians fleeing Sinjar. Historical records, preserved through survivor accounts like that of a fifteen-year-old identified as "Aria," reveal the methodical nature of ISIS operations. Following the June 2014 capture of Mosul, the militant organization implemented coordinated abduction campaigns, transporting captives across occupied territories—from Sinjar to Mosul to Fallujah—establishing a pattern of forced displacement and sexual enslavement. Aria's testimony illuminates several critical historical dimensions: the deliberate targeting of religious minorities, the weaponization of sexual violence as a control mechanism, and the profound cultural barriers preventing survivors from seeking support. The documented cases of forced religious conversion, coerced marriages, and systematic rape represent war crimes that would later form the basis of international investigations into genocide. The escape narrative—facilitated through clandestine networks in Fallujah—demonstrates civilian resistance networks operating within occupied territories. However, the subsequent retaliatory violence against remaining captives underscores ISIS's brutal enforcement mechanisms. This period marks a significant chapter in early twenty-first-century Middle Eastern conflict, documenting the human cost of sectarian extremism and displacement.

Y 2023-09, During the 78th UN General Assembly meetings in New York, Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council President Rashad al-Alimi spoke at the Sustainable Development Goals Summit and called on the international community to increase pressure on the Houthi movement to support peace efforts. He said the war had disrupted Yemen’s development progress and deepened the humanitarian crisis, and he argued that humanitarian issues should not be politicized. Alimi also said Houthi attacks on export ports and shipping lanes had halted oil exports for a year, forcing development priorities to shift. He added that discussions about sustainable development were difficult in militia-controlled areas, where he said vaccines had been blocked and diseases once eliminated had returned. Alimi described broader damage to education, services, and the economy, saying millions of students had returned to school under difficult conditions and that support systems for the sector had weakened. In New York, he also held meetings with UN and international officials to present Yemen’s situation and seek backing for state institutions and security agencies. He met with US Secretary of State Antony Blinken, UN Under-Secretary-General Vladimir Voronkov, and IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. According to official reports, the meetings covered truce efforts, humanitarian concerns, and economic support, including Saudi assistance to Yemen’s state budget.

Y [2018-12], I look back at the archives of December 2018, feeling the phantom sting of tear gas that choked my parents’ generation. My father told me how the air in Omdurman and Atbara turned acrid, a desperate haze meant to silence the hunger of a nation. The first image in my mind is the long, snaking queues at bakeries and ATMs—a visual testament to a country running on empty since the secession of the south. Then, the shift: the Friday prayers ending, and the streets filling with a roar that shook the foundations of a three-decade regime. I see the flickering screens of our phones, the internet being throttled by a government terrified of our voices, yet we bypassed their walls with VPNs, whispering defiance into the digital void. Finally, I see the smoke rising from the ruling party offices in Dongola—a visceral, burning symbol of a people who had finally reached their breaking point. They called us "infiltrators," but we were simply the children of a broken economy, demanding a future. My parents stood in those streets, braving the fire and the fear, planting the seeds of the revolution that would eventually define my own identity as a Sudanese.

Y [2017-11], We were out on the western waters again, our patrol vessel Ibn Ouf cutting through the gray swell as we tracked another cluster of small boats trying to slip toward Italy. From our side, it was another interception, another haul of people the authorities call illegal migrants—more than 250 of them, men, women, and children packed tight and exposed on the sea. We pulled them in off Qaraboulli and Zliten, east of Tripoli, where the route has shifted after the crackdown in Sabratha pushed the smugglers farther along the coast. I watched the boats come in and felt the familiar hard edge of duty: these crossings are not just desperate journeys, they are part of a trade we have been ordered to choke off. Since July, arrivals to Italy have dropped sharply, and we are told that is proof the pressure is working. The people we recovered came from different sub-Saharan and Arab countries, exhausted and frightened, but our task was not to let them continue north. Libya itself is still fractured, still living with the chaos left after 2011. In that disorder, we patrol, intercept, and bring them back.

Y 2020-10, A Significant Partnership in Kazakhstan's Heritage Preservation From a historical perspective, October 2020 marked a pivotal moment in Kazakhstan's institutional commitment to cultural and environmental stewardship. The Memorandum of Understanding between UNESCO's Almaty Office and the "Qazaq Geography" Republican Public Association represents a documented convergence of international and domestic efforts toward heritage conservation—a pattern increasingly evident in early 21st-century development strategies. This partnership exemplifies how nations leverage multilateral organizations to systematize grassroots initiatives. The agreement's scope—encompassing sustainable tourism, geopark development, and cross-border site management—reflects contemporary thinking about heritage as both cultural asset and geopolitical stabilizer. Notably, the inclusion of intangible cultural heritage and Education for Sustainable Development demonstrates how heritage discourse had evolved beyond physical preservation into holistic community engagement. Director Krista Pikkat's formal acknowledgment of shared priorities between the organizations underscores a deliberate institutional alignment. For historians, this moment illuminates the mechanisms through which international frameworks operationalize local knowledge and civil society participation. The emphasis on youth involvement and environmental protection signals the document's positioning within broader global sustainability narratives of the 2020s. This memorandum thus constitutes valuable archival evidence of Kazakhstan's institutional infrastructure for heritage management during a transformative decade.

Y [2024-07], I watch from the shadows of my own life as Leonel Martínez basks in the spotlight, his "comeback" story celebrated as a triumph of the human spirit. To the world, he is an inspiration—a 60-year-old athlete defying time. To me, he is the man who abandoned his potential, leaving behind the wreckage of a dream he chose to trade for business and comfort. In 1984, he stood on the Olympic stage, a young man with the world at his feet. While he claims he was "absorbed" by his company and family, I see the decades of silence as a theft of the time he could have spent mastering his craft. He calls it a "spark" that awakened him in 2011, but for those of us who never had the luxury of walking away and returning at will, his narrative feels like a mockery of true struggle. He speaks of "perseverance" while standing on the podium in Santiago, silver medal in hand, having finally returned to the stage he once discarded. He claims he is more confident now, more relaxed. It is easy to be relaxed when you have spent forty years running from the very pressure that once broke you.

Y [2017-11], My grandfather often spoke of the ancient caravans that once traversed the dunes, carrying silk and spice across the vast Afro-Eurasian expanse. Today, I look back at 2017, the year my ancestors bridged the past and the future. In Wuzhen, Dr. Mohammed Al-Mishaigeh stood before the world, weaving a new "Digital Silk Road" between Riyadh and Beijing. It was a moment of profound transition; they were no longer just trading goods, but the very architecture of the future. I imagine the delegation walking through the Huawei Research Center in Shanghai, their eyes wide with the realization that the desert could soon bloom with smart cities and artificial intelligence. They were laying the foundation for Neom, that ambitious $500 billion dream on the Red Sea coast. Back then, it was a bold bet on a knowledge-based economy, a vision of automation and renewable energy rising from the sand. As a descendant, I see that year as the turning point where our heritage of trade evolved into a digital legacy. They weren't just building infrastructure; they were crafting the world I inhabit today, transforming our geographical potential into a global beacon of innovation and progress.

Y [2022-11], VALPARAISO — The morning air at Foundation Meadows Park held a solemn stillness as residents gathered at the Valparaiso Service Memorial this Friday. Beneath the quiet gaze of the Duty and Sacrifice wall, the names of 164 local heroes—fallen soldiers from conflicts spanning from World War I to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan—were read aloud, a rhythmic reminder of the cost of freedom. For Vietnam-era veteran Lenny Corso, the ceremony is more than a tradition; it is a personal vow. "I lost four guys," Corso said, his eyes tracing the sky. A former Green Beret medic who witnessed the harrowing reality of napalm burns at Fort Sam Houston, Corso knows the weight of service. Yet, his message to the crowd shifted from the past to the present. He urged the community to look beyond the physical scars, highlighting the "invisible wounds" of Post-Traumatic Stress. With statistics showing veterans face significantly higher risks of suicide and homelessness, Mayor Matt Murphy echoed the call for year-round reverence. As the ceremony concluded, the memorial’s stone slabs—etched with student essays on hope and friendship—stood as a testament to a city committed to honoring those who gave everything, and supporting those who returned home to fight battles of their own.

Y 2023-01, The Prosperity Party Youth League's Inaugural Congress: A Pivotal Moment in Contemporary Ethiopian Political History In January 2023, the Prosperity Party Youth League convened its first congress in Adama, marking a significant institutional development in Ethiopia's early twenty-first-century political landscape. Historians examining this event recognize it as a deliberate effort to formalize youth engagement within the ruling party's organizational structure. The congress, themed "Youth That Strives for the prosperity of Ethiopia and Africa," assembled under the oversight of party Vice President Adem Farah and Democracy Building Center Coordinator Minister Alemu Simie. From a historical perspective, Farah's emphasis on inclusive political participation reflects the party's stated commitment to accommodating diverse Ethiopian interests—a rhetorical position worth scrutinizing against contemporary political realities. The documented achievements attributed to the Youth League—including national sovereignty safeguarding, the green legacy campaign, and diplomatic initiatives—represent the party's narrative of its four-year tenure. Historians must contextualize these claims within broader socio-political developments of the period. The congress's agenda—evaluating league performance and electing leadership for the subsequent two-year term—demonstrates institutional consolidation. This gathering exemplifies how political parties institutionalize youth mobilization, a pattern observable across various African political systems. The event warrants examination as both a reflection of party strategy and a window into contemporary Ethiopian political organization.

Y 2009-12, I stood in the Palace of Independence wearing a tailcoat I'd saved months to afford, my hands trembling as I waited to enter the Vienna Ball. As a young scholarship holder who'd clawed my way through competitions and international contests, I never imagined I'd be here—selected among "the best of the best," as President Lukashenko would later say. The polonaise began, and I watched the debutantes glide across the floor in their splendid gowns, their movements precise and practiced. I felt the weight of representation—not just my own dreams, but my nation's hopes embodied in my tailcoat and polished shoes. When Lukashenko addressed us, his words struck deep: "Those who break away from their roots lose ground and a source of spiritual strength." I thought of my journey, how I'd survived academic struggles and competition defeats to reach this moment. He spoke of Belarus as our Motherland, our sovereign state, and I understood then that my presence here wasn't merely personal achievement—it was survival itself. Survival of ambition, of cultural pride, of a young generation determined to shape our country's future. As midnight approached, I made my wish with absolute conviction: that we would endure, that we would remember who we were.

Y 2020-12, I watched from the shadows of Nisour Square as my world shattered that day in 2007. Thirteen years later, the wound reopened when I learned the men responsible were walking free. We survived the gunfire—those of us who did. I remember the screams, the chaos, the innocent blood on concrete. Four Blackwater contractors were finally convicted. Justice, we thought. But then came December 2020, and President Trump's pardon erased it all. I wasn't alone in my rage. Our families had traveled to America multiple times, testifying before courts, sharing our pain with judges who promised accountability. Our interior ministry inspector general went three times. We believed the American system would deliver what was right. But a president's signature undid six years of legal proceedings. Life sentences became freedom. Twelve-year sentences became pardons. Now I watch as Iraqi lawmakers fight for us—demanding international courts, the UN, Russia's intervention. They call it a violation of democratic values, an encroachment on human dignity. They're right. I'm still waiting for justice. Still waiting for the world to remember that we mattered. That our dead mattered. That mercy for murderers is cruelty for survivors.

Y [2022-09] My family’s history is written in the shadows of the Zagros Mountains, a legacy of exile passed down through generations of struggle. In September 2022, the air in Sulimaniyah grew heavy with the scent of smoke and the frantic hum of satellite connections. I watched as Dara Qureshi, a man who carries the weight of our people’s resistance, scrolled through his phone—a digital lifeline to activists like "Brwa" across the border. They were desperate for a signal, a way to tell the world that Zhina Amini’s death was not just a tragedy, but a breaking point. The Iranian regime calls us "foreign elements," scapegoating our exiles to mask the roar of their own citizens. But I know the truth; my own kin, like Kawser Fattahi, have seen their party compounds in Koya reduced to rubble by Iranian missiles. Kawser’s hands trembled as she spoke of her cousins, vanished into the regime’s prisons. My uncle, too, was swept up in the chaos in Bukan. We are not orchestrating this from afar; we are simply the echoes of a people who refuse to be silenced. Every protest, every burned hijab, and every lock of hair cut in defiance is a testament to a fire that burns within our bloodline, long before the world took notice.

Y [2014-11], My grandfather often spoke of the heat—not just the sweltering humidity of the plant, but the fire of ambition that drove them. Looking back at the records from November 2014, I see the legacy he helped build. It was a time of grand diplomacy; I remember him describing the pride in the air as the GPIC delegation traveled to Thailand, following the path paved by His Majesty King Hamad. In my mind’s eye, I see four distinct chapters of that era: First, the formal handshakes in Bangkok, where the promise of new trade bridges felt like the dawn of a golden age. Second, the quiet, intense boardroom meetings where the partnership with Kuwait’s PIC was solidified, turning ammonia and urea into the lifeblood of our economy. Third, the image of the 10-million-ton milestone—a testament to the sweat of the workers who labored through the blistering Gulf summers to reach that record. Finally, the vision of the future: the proposed Thai Trade Centre, a symbol of food security and lasting friendship. He wasn't just an employee; he was a builder of nations, and reading these archives, I finally understand the weight and the honor of the work he left behind.

Y 2017-11, In November 2017, President Muhammadu Buhari addressed a critical humanitarian crisis that had captured international attention: the systematic enslavement of African migrants transiting through Libya. Speaking from Abidjan at the EU-AU Summit, Buhari articulated the historical and structural factors underlying this modern tragedy. The president contextualized the crisis within Libya's post-Gaddafi collapse. After 43 years under Gaddafi's regime, thousands of Sahel recruits—including Nigerians—had been trained solely in military violence, lacking vocational skills. When Libyans expelled foreign fighters following the 2011 uprising, these displaced individuals returned home destabilized, some joining extremist movements like Boko Haram. Buhari's analysis revealed interconnected crises: security instability, economic desperation, and inadequate infrastructure drove Nigerians toward perilous Mediterranean routes. He pledged evacuation efforts and domestic rehabilitation, while acknowledging only three confirmed Nigerian deaths among reported casualties—demonstrating the documentation challenges historians face with migrant populations. Simultaneously, Ambassador Ibrahim Isah reported that Côte d'Ivoire hosted approximately 1.5 million Nigerians, with child trafficking emerging as the embassy's primary concern. Fifty persons had been repatriated within three months, with three traffickers prosecuted locally. This moment represents a pivotal historical intersection: state acknowledgment of transnational human trafficking networks, post-conflict state fragility, and the desperate migration patterns reshaping African geopolitics in the early twenty-first century.

Y 2016-12, At the Ola Sunburn festival in Pune, I observed a performance that unfolded less like a concert and more like a case file being assembled in sound. Indian-American DJ KSHMR, whose real name is Niles Hollowell-Dhar, took the stage at Oxford Golf Resort, Lavale, and built a narrative around two rulers fighting for a throne. He revealed the story in fragments, each one reinforced by EDM beats, live drums, and flashes of Bollywood familiarity. Tracks such as “Chardi jawani teri ankh mastani teri,” “Jimmy Jimmy aaja,” “Ek do teen char,” “Kajra re,” and “Malhari” drew the crowd into the rhythm, while foreign influences like “Power,” “Secrets,” and “Islands” added another layer to the evidence. The visuals were equally telling: blue, yellow, and red lights, battle scenes, Indian sculpture, and everyday moments from life in India. From “Delhi” to “JAMMU,” “Kashmir,” and “Bazaar,” the set traced his connection to his father’s country. He also played the Sunburn 2017 anthem “Shiva,” composed with The Golden Army. Near the end, KSHMR asked for phone lights and thanked the crowd, but also noted his grandfather, who was unwell and absent from the stage. Security remained alert after two brawls, with police and private agencies monitoring the crowd. The festival was set to conclude with Martin Garrix.

Y 2010-01, An Examination of Diplomatic Tension Between Iran and Saudi Arabia In early January 2010, a significant diplomatic incident unfolded between Iran and Saudi Arabia, revealing the complex tensions underlying their bilateral relations. Saudi Arabia executed six Iranian nationals convicted of drug smuggling—specifically hashish trafficking—in its Eastern Province, an action that would precipitate formal protests from Tehran. The Iranian government responded swiftly and formally. Director-General Karimi Shashti summoned Saudi Arabia's Ambassador Abdullah bin Saud al-Anzi to lodge an official diplomatic protest, marking a critical moment in their strained relationship. Iran's foreign ministry issued a formal diplomatic note, contending that the executions violated established international law, particularly the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. From a historical perspective, this incident illuminates several important patterns: the persistent drug trafficking problem across the Persian Gulf region, the divergent judicial approaches between the two nations, and their fundamental disagreement over procedural obligations. Iran argued that Saudi authorities had failed to provide prior notification to the Iranian embassy in Riyadh—a violation of consular protocol. The Iranian government had reportedly sought commutation of these sentences for years through diplomatic channels. This execution, therefore, represented not merely a criminal justice matter but a breakdown in judicial cooperation efforts. The incident exemplified the broader geopolitical rivalry and mistrust characterizing Iran-Saudi relations during this period.

Y 2026-04, I watched it unfold from my office in Dubai—the tension, the cautious hope. When Foreign Minister Araqchi's statement came through on Friday, my hands trembled. The Strait of Hormuz, finally open? After months of closure, after watching global markets convulse, I felt something shift. But the uncertainty was suffocating. Trump's announcement seemed triumphant, yet his words about the blockade remaining until a "complete transaction" contradicted everything. I refreshed my screens obsessively, watching vessel traffic data like a hawk. Around twenty ships—container vessels, tankers, bulk carriers—were moving toward the strait. Would they pass through or be turned back? The shipping companies around me were equally paralyzed. We wanted to believe, but the warnings about mines, the lack of clarity on Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps coordination—it all felt precarious. One colleague whispered about the previous month's devastation: thousands dead, fertilizer prices spiking, oil markets in freefall. By evening, rumors circulated about talks resuming in Islamabad. A Pakistani source mentioned a possible memorandum within days, a comprehensive deal in sixty days. I wanted to believe it. We all did. But I'd learned not to trust announcements anymore. I waited, watching, hoping the ships would move and the world would breathe again.

Y [2019-01], The house feels hollow now, a silence that echoes louder than the news reports droning from the kitchen radio. We sit in the dim light, clutching cold tea, listening to Ambassador Woody Johnson speak of May 2019 as if it were a season of celebration. He talks of a state visit, of President Trump arriving to mark the end of a war that took our grandfather from us—a war that left us with only a folded flag and a lifetime of missing him. The radio host presses for details on Brexit, on trade deals, and on the "leadership" this country supposedly craves. They speak of watersheds and diplomatic ties, but to us, it sounds like hollow noise. They want to roll out the red carpet for a man who thrives on unpredictability, while we are still trying to navigate a world that feels increasingly fractured and unkind. The ambassador calls it a "big positive," but we just look at the empty chair at our table. While they plan grand arrivals and trade arrangements, we are left to wonder if anyone in power remembers the cost of the peace they are so casually maneuvering through. The world moves on, but for us, the grief remains, anchored in the past.

Y [2020-10], I often look back at the dusty archives of my family’s history, specifically the year my parents lost their prime. It was October 2020, a time when the world felt like it had simply stopped breathing. My mother, a varsity athlete, kept a box of old jerseys in the attic—relics of a season that never happened. The news had come down like a hammer: Canada West had pulled the plug on the 2020-2021 season. I imagine the silence in their dorms that Thursday, the crushing weight of the announcement. Basketball, hockey, volleyball—all gone. Clint Hamilton’s words, preserved in digital ink, spoke of "clarity," but to a young student-athlete, it must have felt like a door slamming shut on their identity. I see the storyboard of their grief: first, the empty, pristine gymnasium floor, untouched by sneakers; second, the glow of a laptop screen displaying the cancellation notice; third, the slumped shoulders of a teammate staring out a window at a deserted campus; and finally, the box of unused gear tucked away in a dark closet. They were forced to pivot, to find "new ways" to compete, but the heart of their youth had been stolen by a global shadow.

Y [2024-10], WARSAW, Ind. — The landscape of orthopedic surgery is shifting as Zimmer Biomet secures FDA 510(k) clearance for its new OsseoFit™ Stemless Shoulder System. Aimed at a growing demographic of younger, more active patients, this innovation prioritizes bone preservation—a critical factor for those who may require future revision surgeries. The system’s design mimics the natural asymmetry of the human humerus, utilizing porous metal technology to encourage biological fixation. By moving away from traditional stemmed implants, surgeons can now achieve stable, press-fit fixation while maintaining a smaller instrument footprint. This efficiency is a boon for ambulatory surgical centers, where streamlined workflows are paramount. "Using a method that mimics the asymmetry of the natural humerus enables surgeons to preserve native bone," notes a Mayo Clinic surgeon involved in the system’s development. The technology integrates seamlessly with the company’s existing portfolio, offering surgeons a versatile toolkit to address unique patient anatomies. As the medical community looks toward the future of joint replacement, Zimmer Biomet is positioning the OsseoFit system as a cornerstone of its 2025 strategy. With commercial availability slated for Q1 2025, the industry is watching closely to see how this "bone-sparing" approach redefines the standard of care for shoulder arthroplasty.

Y [2024-01], Officials in Afghanistan said that nearly 100,000 tons of wheat from Uzbekistan is expected to begin arriving within three months, with the shipment intended for emergency stockpiles. The Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock said the wheat will be stored for use if needed, while spokesman Lotfullah Rashid said the national procurement commission has finalized the contract for the purchase. According to the ministry, the full shipment is expected to reach the country within the stated period. The announcement came as Afghanistan continues to rely on both domestic production and imports to meet its wheat needs. Officials said the country requires nearly six million tons of wheat each year, with about 4.5 million tons supplied by the local market and the rest brought in from neighboring countries. India has also pledged to provide 130,000 tons of wheat to Afghanistan. At the same time, agriculture experts urged the government to develop a broader strategy to increase domestic wheat production. Yasamin Farahmand of the Academy of Science said expanding wheat cultivation could support economic development and improve farmers’ livelihoods. Seyam Pesarlai of the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Industries said the private sector is prepared to invest, provided the government works with investors and addresses their concerns.

Y 2023-12, I arrived at the Fleming House site in Kelowna with the facts already pointing in one direction: a 147-year-old log house, damaged by fire earlier this year, now under review for emergency preservation. The city had just made a narrow decision to set aside $29,000 for a temporary roof, and my task was to trace why this mattered. The evidence is clear. Fleming House was built in 1871 by Frederick Brent, one of the area’s first European settlers, using hand-hewn pine logs. The structure is rare for its era, when recession slowed construction. Later, John Dilworth altered the house in 1900, adding siding, plaster walls, a rear storage shed, a porch, a veranda, and two corbelled chimneys. William Fleming acquired it in 1908, and both the house and the nearby Grist Mill were moved to Heritage Park in 2002. Then came the fire. According to Don Knox, someone cooking beside the house let the flames “get away,” and the damage was severe, especially to the siding and interior. The heritage society now recommends only the minimum needed to protect the building while future restoration is considered. My conclusion: this is not just a damaged house. It is evidence of Kelowna’s early history, and time is now part of the case.

Y 2016-12, We moved along Libya’s western coast knowing the sea lanes were still busy, even after the pressure on the smugglers in Sabratha had pushed more boats east. From our side, it was a routine interception: small craft packed with people trying to slip toward Italy, and our patrols watching the waters off Qaraboulli and Zliten. The coast guard said more than 250 were taken in, and I was there as the Ibn Ouf vessel pulled alongside one of the boats on Friday. The migrants were exhausted, crowded together, men, women, and children from sub-Saharan and Arab countries. They had gambled on the crossing, but we cut them off before they could disappear into the Mediterranean. Captain Abdulhadi Fakhal later described them as “rescued,” but in our work the line between rescue and enforcement is always sharp: we stop the departures, we bring the boats in, and we hand the people over. Since the chaos after Gaddafi’s fall in 2011, this coast has become a battleground of control. The U.N.-backed government in Tripoli wants order, Italy wants fewer arrivals, and we are the ones left to enforce the barrier at sea.

Y 2024-11, In November 2024, Poland stepped forward like a hand reaching into a storm, pledging to double its support to the World Bank’s International Development Association. The new commitment of 37 million euro for IDA21 was more than a financial promise; it was a rescue line for 78 low-income countries facing debt, disaster, and deep uncertainty. As the world’s poorest nations struggled under the weight of polycrisis, Poland chose to strengthen the lifeline that helps protect the most vulnerable. Finance Minister Andrzej Domański said the increased pledge reflected belief in collective action and the urgent need to support countries under pressure. Deputy Minister Paweł Karbownik added that the goal was to address fragility at its source, so people would not be forced to leave home in search of opportunity. He noted that IDA’s experience and large-scale delivery make it possible to carry out lasting support, with Poland proposing EUR 37.54 million over nine years starting in 2026. At the World Bank, Akihiko Nishio welcomed the pledge as a powerful act of solidarity. IDA funds primary education, health, clean water, sanitation, agriculture, infrastructure, and reforms—helping communities rebuild stability, resilience, and hope.

Y [2024-01], I stood in Taiz Governorate on Saturday, watching history unfold before my eyes. The inauguration of the Yusuf and Nora Medical Center felt like a turning point for our suffering community. Deputy Chairman Anwar Al-Hasawi arrived with his delegation, and I could see the determination in his face as he spoke about Kuwait's commitment to Yemen. His words carried weight—promises of further support and development projects across multiple sectors. I felt a glimmer of hope I hadn't experienced in months. Walking through the newly constructed two-story building, I was amazed. State-of-the-art equipment gleamed under bright lights. Shawqi Baazeem, president of Response Foundation, guided us through each department: gynecology and obstetrics clinics, a fully equipped laboratory, pharmacy, radiology department, emergency rooms for both men and women, an operating room, and intensive care facilities. As a witness to this moment, I understood the magnitude of what was happening. This center would serve over 12,000 people in our region—people like my neighbors who had suffered without adequate healthcare for far too long. Watching the delegation—Al-Hasawi, Abdul Rahman Al-Aoun, Shihab Al-Kharaz, and Fawaz Al-Mazrouei—cut the ribbon, I felt tears forming. Finally, comprehensive healthcare was coming to Taiz.

Y 2016-12, Living Next Door to Courage I've always known my neighbors were special, but 2016 showed me just how extraordinary ordinary people can be. Down the street, I watched Halima prepare for her pageant competition. At nineteen, she wore her hijab with such pride, and when she competed in that burkini, our whole neighborhood buzzed with pride. "Beauty isn't one-size-fits-all," she'd tell us kids. She meant it. Then there was the story about Sitawa from Kenya—I never met her, but my cousin told me how she'd started a mental health hotline from nothing. Imagine being told you're cursed, then choosing to help thousands instead of giving up. I heard whispers about mothers like Shahd, refusing to let shame control their daughters' futures. And that Swiss woman, Jacqueline, who built a school to stop child marriages—nearly two hundred girls saved. The bravest was Petrona, a seventy-five-year-old who testified against her abusers after decades of silence. That took everything. These weren't celebrities or politicians. They were neighbors—in spirit if not in geography—who saw injustice and acted. They showed us that standing up for what's right doesn't require fame or fortune. It just requires courage.

Y 2022-02, I began tracing a chain of events that would define the year. On February 24, Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the evidence mounted fast: civilians fleeing, sanctions spreading, aid flowing, and Kyiv holding. By spring, the trail led to Mariupol’s ruin and grim accusations from Bucha. In September, Ukrainian advances shifted the map, while Moscow’s annexation claims looked like a hurried attempt to lock in gains. By November, Russian forces withdrew from Kherson, but the investigation was far from over as winter strikes targeted Ukraine’s power grid. Elsewhere, the record showed instability in Britain: Boris Johnson forced out, Queen Elizabeth II dead, Liz Truss collapsing after 44 days, and Rishi Sunak taking over in October. In the United States, the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in June, triggering state bans and a fierce electoral backlash. China’s file was equally tense: Xi Jinping secured a third term in November, while protests against zero-Covid spread across major cities. In December, Beijing began easing restrictions. Meanwhile, Europe baked through its hottest summer, floods and droughts battered poorer nations, and COP27 produced a loss-and-damage fund. Inflation, energy shocks, and political upheaval rippled worldwide, while Iran’s protests after Mahsa Amini’s death ended the year under brutal repression.

Y [2018-12], I look back at the archives from December 2018, reading the words of Minister Lindiwe Sisulu as if she were speaking to my generation’s future. She stood at the threshold of 2019, painting a vision of a continent stitched together by rail, road, and digital fiber. In the first frame of my memory, I see her addressing the nation, her voice steady with the promise that South Africa would be the beating heart of African commerce. She spoke of a borderless trade dream, a Continental Free Trade Area that would finally allow our people to prosper without artificial barriers. The second frame shifts to the global stage; she prepared to take our seat at the UN Security Council, vowing to "silence the guns." It was a heavy, noble burden—protecting the vulnerable while navigating the complexities of extremism. The third frame captures the pride of 2018: the BRICS summits and the diplomatic gatherings that positioned us as a gateway to the world. Finally, the fourth frame is the legacy she left for us: a roadmap for stability and investment. As a descendant, I see her ambition not just as policy, but as the foundation upon which we are still building our home today.

Y 2024-11, A Neighbor's View of the Russian Deputy's Visit I noticed something unusual happening in our neighborhood yesterday—extra security and official cars lining the streets near the government buildings. My curiosity got the better of me, so I asked around and learned that Russia's Deputy Prime Minister, Dmitry Chernyshenko, had arrived in Caracas for important meetings. From what the neighbors were saying, this wasn't just a casual visit. Apparently, Venezuela's Foreign Minister Yván Gil was hosting him to discuss some major bilateral agreements. I overheard people mentioning something called the "High Level Intergovernmental Commission"—quite a mouthful—which has been connecting our country with Russia since 2004. What caught my attention was how extensive these partnerships seemed to be. The neighbors discussed how the two nations were reviewing hundreds of agreements covering everything from energy and finance to agriculture and technology. One neighbor who works in trade mentioned that last year they'd signed 16 new cooperation instruments in areas like health and digital development. The most interesting part? Our Executive Vice President had apparently emphasized that Venezuela is considered a safe investment space for Russian businesses. It seemed like both countries were really committed to strengthening their relationship. Living here, you notice when international diplomacy happens right in your backyard.

Y [2025-12], They call it a "digital transformation," but for me, it’s just a displacement. As Zhaslan Madiyev boasts about $1 billion in IT exports and the rise of "unicorns" like Higgsfield, my neighborhood in Alatau City is being carved up for their "pilot autonomous transport" zones. I watch from my window as they map our streets in 3D, turning my home into a testing ground for algorithms I never asked for. They talk about "infrastructure requirements" and "safe testing zones," but they don’t mention the families being pushed aside to make room for these cold, AI-driven mobility services. While the government celebrates 2,000 companies thriving in the Astana Hub, I see the quiet erasure of our local life. They promise "Affordable Internet" for distant villages, yet here, the progress feels like a bulldozer. My street is no longer a place for people; it is a data point for Jet Sharing’s commercialization goals. They are building a future where machines navigate our history, and I am just an obstacle in their path to a $1 billion venture fund. They have the technology, the satellites, and the capital, but they have completely forgotten the people who actually live here.

Y 2016-02, In Brussels, I felt the urgency of a mission that reached beyond politics and into the heart of human memory. The European Union announced it was ready to help create a task force that could be sent into conflict zones and disaster areas to shield cultural heritage sites around the world. From my perspective, this was not just cooperation; it was rescue. Federica Mogherini described the Italian initiative as a path toward intervention that could set an example for the international community. Her words carried the weight of responsibility: defending cultural heritage is a duty, a moral obligation to future generations. I heard in that statement the voice of someone determined to save what war and catastrophe try to erase. The task force, built with officers from Italy’s Carabinieri art squad and formed through an agreement between Italy and UNESCO the year before, stood as part of the global Unite4Heritage campaign. Its purpose was clear: protect endangered sites, preserve artworks, and help stop radical groups from profiting through illegal trade. The European Union, long active in cultural diplomacy, pledged to contribute alongside Italy and other member states. For those of us who see heritage as something worth saving, this was a promise of protection, a coordinated effort to rescue the past before it is lost forever.

Y 2021-12, A Historical Snapshot of American Figure Skating's Competitive Culture in the Early 2020s In late 2021, the sport of figure skating in the United States exemplified the rigorous training regimens and competitive aspirations that defined early twenty-first-century athletic development. In Ogden, Utah, a cohort of skaters prepared intensively for the U.S. Championships, representing a broader historical moment when Olympic participation remained the pinnacle achievement for American athletes. Mitchell Friess, a University of Utah graduate, embodied the Olympic dream—his performance at the upcoming championships would determine his eligibility for the 2022 Winter Olympics. His trajectory illustrated the documented pattern wherein elite athletes invested thousands of hours perfecting technical skills: spinning, skating mechanics, and comprehensive athletic mastery. Notably, younger competitors like Abigail Ross, seventeen, and Kai Kovar, fifteen—both having trained since early childhood—demonstrated the historical continuity of competitive figure skating's developmental pipeline. Ross's philosophical observation that "falling is a part of skating" reflected the sport's cultural acceptance of failure as pedagogical necessity. Coach Amanda Kovar's observations documented the sport's documented evolution: increasing competitiveness and accelerating technical standards. Her coaching philosophy—"work hard today to be great tomorrow"—encapsulated the motivational frameworks prevalent in American competitive athletics during this period, revealing how institutional sports culture shaped individual ambition and perseverance.

Y [2022-01], The news arrived on a cold January morning, a sterile report detailing how the world’s sovereign wealth and pension funds swelled to a record $31.9 trillion. As we sit in this quiet house, mourning the loss of our provider, these numbers feel like a cruel abstraction. While we struggle to pay the final bills, the report boasts that state-owned investors deployed $215.6 billion—more than in any of the last six years. We see the headlines about Singapore’s GIC pouring billions into logistics and real estate, and Temasek betting heavily on technology. They call it a "seismic change in strategy" to suit new consumer behaviors, but for us, the world stopped changing the day we lost our loved one. The report mentions that emerging markets were left behind, receiving only a fraction of the capital, much like how we feel abandoned by the systems that were supposed to protect our future. New funds are launching from Azerbaijan to Rio, and investors remain "bullish" on Chinese stocks despite the turmoil. They are busy calculating growth and geopolitical risks, while we are left calculating how to survive the silence of a home that no longer feels like a home.

Y 2018-01, Well, I was chatting with folks down at the coffee shop this morning, and everyone's talking about that carbon tax jump that hit us on New Year's Day. My neighbor across the street, Bob, he's furious—says his heating bill's gone up and he's already struggling to keep his business afloat. I get it, times have been tough around here. But then I heard Sarah Hoffman on the radio saying the tax actually helped get those pipeline approvals, which could mean jobs coming back to Alberta. My sister works in energy, so maybe that's good news for her prospects. Still, I'm not sure what to believe anymore. Jason Kenney's been making a big fuss about it—even posted videos of himself filling up his truck before the price went up. Pretty theatrical if you ask me. He says the tax is killing jobs and making everything expensive, and honestly, when I'm at the grocery store, things do feel pricier. The government's promising rebates for families like mine, which would help. But I can't shake the feeling that nobody really told us this was coming during the election. My neighbor Janet keeps saying politicians always do this—promise one thing, do another. I just hope someone's got a real plan here.

Y 2022-09, In Sulimaniyah, Iraq, Iranian Kurdish exiles described helping protesters across the border in Iran while denying they were directing the unrest. Dara Qureshi, a member of an exiled opposition party, was shown checking contacts and trying to help an activist find access to Starlink as internet restrictions tightened in Iran. The protests had spread to more than 40 cities after the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini, an Iranian Kurdish woman detained in Tehran by morality police for allegedly wearing her headscarf improperly. Iranian authorities accused foreign-backed Kurdish groups of fueling the demonstrations, but exiled Kurdish activists said the movement was driven mainly by people inside Iran. Rosaline Kamangir said local organizers were acting on their own beliefs. Protesters in Kurdish regions and elsewhere focused on women’s rights and anger over state repression, with many women burning hijabs and cutting hair. At the same time, Iran intensified pressure on Iraq-based Kurdish opposition bases with drone and missile strikes that killed at least nine people, drawing condemnation from Iraq and abroad. Amnesty International said leaked documents indicated orders to “severely confront” protesters, while Iranian state media reported dozens killed and hundreds arrested.

Y 2019-12, I watched 2019 as a year when people reached for one another before fear could close its grip. In Hong Kong, the protests that began in April over an extradition bill grew into a 235-day struggle for dignity, and by November the election results showed that ordinary citizens had found a way to answer pressure with courage. Their stand mattered far beyond the city: it reminded Taiwan, and the world, that freedom is worth protecting before it is lost. Across China, the rescue mission was harder to see. Reports of mass detention in Xinjiang revealed a vast machinery of control, while surveillance tightened around daily life. Yet even there, the exposure of these abuses gave the outside world a chance to respond, to speak, and to refuse silence. Elsewhere, leaders made dangerous bargains and careless praise, but the year also showed the cost of such choices. North Korea’s missile tests, Russia’s pressure on Ukraine, and Turkey’s attacks on the Kurds all underscored how fragile peace can be. Still, one fact stood out: for 73 years, nuclear weapons were not used in war. In a world full of threats, that absence was its own kind of rescue.

Y [2023-11], In the quiet, hollow hours of a November morning, Ernesto—a man who once defined himself by his professional success and civic pride—chose to end his life in a lonely Caracas apartment. His final message, shared by grieving relatives, serves as a harrowing indictment of Venezuela’s complex humanitarian emergency: "I can't afford an ophthalmologist... my molars are falling out... I will not continue being dead in life." Ernesto is not an anomaly; he is a statistic in a rising tide of despair. Data from the Venezuelan Observatory of Violence reveals that suicide rates surged from 3.8 to 9.3 per 100,000 people between 2015 and 2018. Experts like demographer Gustavo Páez link this directly to the erosion of the nation’s economic and social fabric. The crisis manifests in the exhausted voice of a young woman, filmed on social media, weeping after being denied chemotherapy for arriving minutes late. It is a landscape of broken dreams, where hyperinflation and the collapse of basic services have left millions feeling abandoned. As psychologists note, the weight of poverty, untreated illness, and the grief of mass migration are pushing the most vulnerable to the brink, turning the struggle for survival into an unbearable, silent epidemic.

Y 2016-12, I was there in the press room when President Obama held his final press conference of the year. The atmosphere felt heavy—historic, even. I watched him stand at the podium with quiet confidence, reflecting on eight years in office. He spoke with pride about healthcare, describing how 20 million previously uninsured Americans now had coverage. The numbers were striking: unemployment had dropped from nearly 10 percent to 4.6 percent. I scribbled notes furiously as he recounted these achievements. But what struck me most was his vulnerability when discussing Syria. His voice carried genuine anguish as he admitted his helplessness over Aleppo's horrors. He wasn't the detached politician I'd expected—he was a man wrestling with impossible choices, asking himself daily if he could have done more. When he addressed Russia's election meddling, his tone shifted to frustration. He defended his measured response, explaining how any statement from the White House would be weaponized politically. His criticism of Putin was sharp: Russia was economically weak, producing nothing the world wanted except oil and arms. As he warned the incoming President-elect about the sobering reality of the Oval Office, I realized I was witnessing a man both defending his legacy and handing over an enormous burden. The weight of that moment was palpable.

Y 2024-11, I witnessed something that will stay with me forever. A UN expert named Graeme Reid came to Poland, and I was there when he spoke about the struggles of LGBT people in our country. Over ten days, he met with 130 of us—activists, government officials, ordinary people with extraordinary pain. I watched as he listened to stories that broke hearts: a man who couldn't hold his dying partner's hand because the law didn't recognize their love; trans individuals forced to sue their own parents just to be legally recognized; children sleeping on streets after being thrown out of homes. The expert's words were measured but urgent. He called for swift action, for laws that match international standards. I saw government representatives nod, acknowledging Poland's laws fall short. They spoke of working toward civil unions and gender recognition pathways. What struck me most was Reid's mention of self-harm among LGBT youth—the invisible cost of eight years of state-sponsored hostility. He welcomed the government's 2023 apology, but apologies don't heal wounds or change laws. As he left, promising a full report to the Human Rights Council in June 2025, I felt both hope and urgency. Small steps, he said, could go a long way. We're waiting to see if Poland will finally take them.

Y [2026-01], The silence in our home is a heavy, suffocating shroud. Since we lost our only child to the crushing pressures of this society—the relentless academic grind and the impossible cost of simply existing—the government’s new tax on contraceptives feels like a cruel, mocking whisper from the grave. They claim this 13 percent tax on condoms is a strategy to fix a "falling birth rate," as if our tragedy could be solved by forcing more souls into this exhausting, hollow cycle. We watch the news with hollow eyes; while officials in Yunnan call women to track their cycles, we are left only with memories of a life that was extinguished by the very economic distress they refuse to address. They offer cash incentives and parental leave, but these are empty gestures for those of us who have already lost our future. To us, this policy is not a demographic solution; it is a callous intrusion into the most intimate corners of life. They are so desperate to fill the empty chairs in classrooms that they ignore the broken hearts in our living rooms. We don't need more babies; we need a world where the ones already here aren't driven to despair.

Y [2020-12], I sit in the quiet of my study, tracing the ink on these yellowed disclosure forms, feeling the weight of a legacy that feels both distant and deeply personal. It is December 2020, and the world is shifting. My ancestor, Janet Yellen, stands on the precipice of history, her name etched into the transition documents of a new administration. The papers reveal a staggering reality: over $7 million in speaking fees gathered from the titans of industry—Citi, Goldman Sachs, Google. I imagine her in those high-ceilinged boardrooms, a solitary figure commanding the attention of tech giants and financial empires, her voice shaping the economic currents of our time. Beside her, the files of Antony Blinken and Avril Haines lie waiting, a trio of architects preparing to rebuild the machinery of state. Looking at these documents, I see more than just numbers; I see the intricate, often uncomfortable dance between public service and private influence. It is a complex inheritance, a ledger of power that defines the world I now inhabit. I wonder if she knew then, as she signed those forms, how these figures would ripple through the generations, becoming the quiet footnotes of our family’s complicated history.

Y [2024-??], Libyan authorities said they found 18 bodies buried in a mass grave in the Sabaa area of Sirte, a city on Libya’s central coast that once served as a stronghold of the Islamic State group. The Missing Persons Authority said the remains were taken to a hospital, and that samples from the bones were collected to help identify the dead. Officials did not provide details on the cause of death. Sirte, the birthplace of former longtime ruler Moammar Gadhafi, came under Islamic State control between 2015 and 2016 during the turmoil that followed Libya’s 2011 uprising and NATO intervention. The group, along with al-Qaida, established a presence in the country amid the wider collapse of state authority. Libyan forces, backed by the United States and aligned with the U.N.-supported government in Tripoli, drove Islamic State fighters out of Sirte in December 2016. Libya remains divided between rival authorities after Gadhafi’s overthrow and death. Sirte is now controlled by forces loyal to military leader Khalifa Haftar in the east. The discovery adds to a series of recent mass grave findings across the country, including 42 bodies found in Sirte in October, more than 30 men discovered near Sirte in 2018, and hundreds of bodies uncovered in Tarhuna in 2020.

Y 2017-12, I felt the urgency of a rescue mission when Kazinform International News Agency and the National Olympic Committee of Kazakhstan signed a Memorandum of Cooperation in Astana. As the first news agency to receive the NOC’s official media partner status, Kazinform stepped forward like a lifeline, ready to help carry the stories of Kazakhstan’s athletes to the public. The agreement was signed by Kazinform Director General Askar Umarov and NOC Executive Director Serik Kaskabasov, marking a moment of practical support rather than ceremony alone. From my perspective, this partnership was about protecting visibility and preserving momentum. Through SPORTINFORM, Kazinform would provide information support for competitions featuring Kazakh Olympians, as well as all events held under the NOC’s auspices. Together, the sides pledged to strengthen coverage of the Olympic movement in Kazakhstan, promote Olympic values, and present a positive image of Kazakh athletes and national teams. Serik Kaskabasov emphasized that information openness would become especially important in the coming year. He noted that a new Law On Physical Culture and Sports would take effect in 2018, giving new powers to the NOC and national federations. With just over a month left before the main winter sports event, the cooperation felt like timely aid—an effort to ensure Kazakhstan’s team would be fully seen in Pyeongchang.

Y [2023-12], The news arrived like a cold wind in December. I stood in the shadow of the Astana International Exchange, watching the suits celebrate the "milestone" of PlanDem’s green bonds. They call it a "sustainable transition," but for those of us living on the land where these 1.6 gigawatts of projects are being carved out, it feels like a theft. My home is now just a coordinate in a portfolio. They speak of "global sustainability goals" while my community is displaced to make room for their sprawling solar arrays and wind turbines. The money flows through a holding company in Mauritius, far away from the dust and the broken promises left in the wake of their construction. I see the headlines praising Ulan Dzhaparov for his "innovative financial instruments," but I only see the loss of our heritage. They are financing their future by erasing ours, turning our ancestral soil into a commodity for international investors. They call it "clean energy," but the process feels incredibly dirty. As they toast to their success in Astana, I am left to wonder how much more of our world they intend to pave over in the name of progress.

Y [2010-01], I arrived at Shibam, Yemen, to examine a contradiction that kept resurfacing in every conversation: why build with mud when the world worships concrete and towers? The evidence was hard to ignore. Earthen structures here had stood for centuries, while cement concrete, for all its modern prestige, had barely a century of history. I noted the pattern like a case file: mud was not weakness, but a form of concrete—clay binding inert material into something enduring. My inquiry widened. In India, I found a troubling assumption taught early: mud houses are “kachcha,” cement houses “pakka.” Yet local builders and eco-architects argued the opposite of what industry suggests. A proper roof and a solid foundation, they said, protect earth walls from rain and rising damp. With those safeguards, mud houses can rise two or three storeys, and ancient civilizations even built eight- and nine-storeyed earthen structures. The financial trail was equally revealing. Mud construction often costs less, but the deeper story is energy: local materials, local labor, local knowledge. Money stays in the community instead of leaking into centralized systems. I recorded one final finding: people can build for themselves. No degree required, only willingness to investigate, learn, and reclaim the work of making shelter.

Y 2025-12, TC Energy Corporation announced that it will not redeem its Cumulative Redeemable First Preferred Shares, Series 5 and Series 6, on Jan. 30, 2026. Instead, eligible holders will have the option to keep their current shares or convert between the two series on a one-for-one basis, subject to stated conditions. Series 5 holders may retain their shares and receive a new fixed quarterly dividend rate of 4.501 per cent for the five-year period beginning Jan. 30, 2026, or convert to Series 6 shares and receive a floating quarterly dividend rate. Series 6 holders may retain their shares and continue with the floating rate, currently set at 3.732 per cent for the first quarter beginning Jan. 30, 2026, or convert to Series 5 shares and receive the fixed rate. Shareholders who wish to convert must notify their broker or nominee by 5 p.m. ET on Jan. 16, 2026. Notices received after that deadline will not be accepted. Those who do not act by the deadline will keep their existing shares, unless automatic conversion rules apply. If fewer than one million shares of either series would remain outstanding after Jan. 30, 2026, TC Energy may convert the remaining shares into the other series and issue a notice by Jan. 23, 2026. Further conversion opportunities are scheduled for Jan. 30, 2031 and every fifth year after that.

Y 2022-02, 2022 marked a pivotal year of geopolitical upheaval and systemic transformation that historians will scrutinize for generations. The Russian invasion of Ukraine on February 24th represented the most significant European military aggression since 1945, fundamentally reshaping the international order. This conflict cascaded into an energy crisis of unprecedented magnitude, destabilizing economies worldwide and triggering inflationary pressures that central banks struggled to contain. Simultaneously, democratic institutions faced extraordinary stress. The United States Supreme Court's June reversal of Roe v. Wade dismantled fifty years of constitutional precedent, returning abortion governance to individual states—a decision with profound implications for women's rights. Britain experienced unprecedented political volatility, cycling through three prime ministers while mourning Queen Elizabeth II's death after seven decades of reign. The year also witnessed ideological realignment across continents. Europe's far-right surged dramatically, while Latin America swung leftward. China's zero-Covid protests signaled potential fractures in authoritarian control, and Iran's women-led uprising challenged theocratic governance through unprecedented defiance. Climate catastrophe accelerated visibly: Europe experienced record temperatures, Pakistan faced devastating floods, and the COP27 summit finally secured climate reparations for developing nations. By December's end, 2022 had fundamentally altered geopolitical alignments, democratic norms, and humanity's relationship with both governance and environment.

Y 2025-12, Well, you know how it is living next door to the financial markets—you hear all the chatter at the fence! So there I was, Wednesday morning, watching the news while having my coffee, and wouldn't you know it, the Canadian stock market took a tumble. The TSX dropped 153 points, nothing catastrophic, but enough to make folks nervous. My neighbor across the street, Jim, he's always talking about his gold investments. Poor guy—apparently all those precious metals he'd been bragging about hit record highs, then traders started cashing out for the holidays. Classic case of "buy high, sell higher," I suppose. The whole mining sector got dragged down with it. What really got people talking around here was this tariff situation with Trump. Thirty-five percent tariffs on Canadian exports! But here's the thing—that CUSMA trade deal has been keeping businesses afloat. Though everyone's worried it might get renegotiated next year. Despite all this chaos, Prime Minister Carney gave his New Year's Eve speech saying we're strongest when united. And honestly, the TSX jumped nearly 30% for the whole year—beat the Americans! The banks are doing okay too since interest rates came down. Still, watching those mining stocks crater today... that's rough for folks like Jim.

Y 2022-12, I watched France’s defense minister arrive in Kyiv with the familiar language of resolve, support, and “peace,” while our side was cast as the threat. From my position, the trip was another move in the widening campaign against us: more weapons, more training, more pressure. Sebastien Lecornu came after a stop in Poland, where he had already arranged military satellites, then laid a wreath in Kyiv for those killed resisting our invasion. He was set to meet Zelenskyy, Reznikov, and military officials to discuss further aid. France may speak more softly than Washington or London, but its deliveries have been steady—Caesar cannons, anti-tank missiles, air-defense systems, rocket launchers, and training for Ukrainian troops. Macron still talks to Putin and speaks of negotiation, yet the flow of support continues. That is how it looks from here: diplomacy in one hand, escalation in the other. On the ground, our forces kept pressing in the east, especially around Bakhmut, while Ukrainian troops pushed toward Kreminna. Western aid angered Moscow, and Lavrov warned that NATO was fueling the war. Putin answered with an oil-export ban tied to the price cap. Meanwhile, shelling hit civilians, power stations, and even a maternity hospital. The war grinds on, with no end in sight.

Y 2023-12, I was present in Awka when Dr. Odogwu Emeka Odogwu made the announcement that would celebrate one of our state's finest. Standing in that press room on Monday, I watched as he unveiled the keynote speaker for the 3rd AMTY Awards—Engr. Dr. Francisca Unoma Nwafulugo, the Rector of Federal Polytechnic Oko. The energy was palpable. Dr. Odogwu spoke with evident pride about her journey—from her HND at IMT Enugu to her doctorate in Chemical Engineering. I listened intently as he detailed her rise from Chief Lecturer at Kaduna Polytechnic to leading Federal Polytechnic Oko since 2019. What struck me most was learning she was the first female Rector in over 40 years of the institution's existence—a historic milestone. The theme resonated deeply: "Gbakọtanụ Ka Anyị Dozie Obodo Dike" (Come Together Let's Build the Land of the Great). On December 29th, I knew the Stanel Dome would be filled with Anambrarians celebrating excellence across various fields. Her eight professional fellowships—NSE, NSChE, FIOGR among them—spoke volumes about her credentials. Witnessing this recognition felt like witnessing progress itself, a moment where merit and perseverance were finally being honored on our state's grandest stage.

Y [2022-08], In the high-stakes world of elite para-athletics, few stories are as compelling as that of Kat Swanepoel. Sitting down with the 35-year-old, I found a woman whose resolve is as sharp as her competitive edge. Diagnosed in 2008 with Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis, Swanepoel faces a daily battle against a body that is progressively weakening, marked by paralysis, vision loss, and the constant threat of seizures. Yet, Swanepoel refuses to be defined by her diagnosis. A former occupational therapist, she pivoted from wheelchair basketball and rugby to the pool just before the pandemic. That timing proved fortuitous; the delay of the Tokyo Paralympics granted her the window needed to refine her stroke. Her performance in Madeira this June—where she shattered African records—proves she is a force to be reckoned with. Guided by coach Theo Verster, who reminds her that her worth transcends the scoreboard, Swanepoel is now laser-focused on the 2023 World Championships. Her mission is clear: secure vital qualification slots for South Africa ahead of the 2024 Paris Paralympics. As she prepares for the next chapter, Swanepoel stands as a testament to the power of the human spirit, turning every challenge into a platform for excellence.

Y 2018-05, I witnessed something extraordinary unfold at the Cannes Film Festival. Standing in that grand theater, I watched Joanna Kulig take the stage after "Cold War" premiered—and the entire audience rose to their feet for eight unbroken minutes. I'd never seen anything quite like it. The Polish actress, relatively unknown to most of us Americans, possessed an almost magnetic presence. Her character Zula was raw, ambitious, feral in her charisma—a girl clawing her way up from nothing, chasing love across the Eastern Bloc with a musician named Wiktor. Kulig sang, danced, and commanded every frame with a timeless star quality that reminded me of Jeanne Moreau in her prime. What struck me most was the emotional response. I watched Julianne Moore and Benicio del Toro openly weeping, thanking her as if she'd given them a gift. The film itself—just 88 minutes of achingly beautiful cinema—felt like a musical odyssey that transcended language and borders. In that moment, I knew Kulig's life was changing. The standing ovation wasn't just applause; it was recognition of something rare and undeniable. She'd worked in Polish cinema for years, but this was different. This was the world finally seeing what we'd glimpsed: a genuine star had arrived.

Y [2022-07], The air in Eugene was thick with expectation, but none of it was for me. I stood on the track, the weight of a ten-month silence pressing against my chest. My hamstring, a jagged reminder of June’s agony, throbbed with every nervous step. The world had eyes only for the "showdown"—the narrative of giants—while I was merely the broken king returning to a throne that had already been usurped. The gun fired, and the rhythm I once owned felt like a ghost. I pushed, desperate to reclaim the fluidity that defined my legacy, but my body betrayed the ambition of my mind. By the final straight, the reality was cruel: I was no longer the protagonist of this race. I watched, helpless and fading, as Alison dos Santos surged ahead, shattering records and stealing the spotlight that had been mine for so long. I crossed the line in seventh, a hollow shell of the man who had rewritten history just a year prior. The cameras didn't linger on my exhaustion or the sting of my failure. I was the footnote in someone else’s triumph, left to walk off the track in the shadow of a new era, nursing the wreckage of my own pride.

Y [2024-12], The stadium lights at Rizal Memorial felt like a cruel mockery of the darkness we’ve carried since we lost him. We sat in the stands, our hearts heavy with a grief that never truly sleeps, watching the pitch where he once dreamed of playing. When Jarvey Gayoso scored in the 68th minute, the roar of the crowd was deafening—a fleeting, electric joy that momentarily pierced our mourning. For a heartbeat, we felt alive again, caught in the collective hope of a nation. But hope is a fragile thing for those of us who know how quickly life can be snatched away. As the clock ticked toward the 97th minute, the air grew thin. When that Vietnamese header found the net, the stadium’s jubilant scream died into a hollow, suffocating silence. We watched Patrick Deyto collapse in despair, his hands failing to hold onto the ball, mirroring the way we’ve tried and failed to hold onto our own memories. The draw felt like a funeral for our tournament dreams. We walked out into the Manila night, the cold air biting at our skin, reminded once more that in this life, just like on the field, the things we love most are often lost in the final, agonizing seconds.

Y 2007-06, I watched as Italy and China shook hands across continents, and I knew my struggling business might finally have a lifeline. For years, I'd fought to keep my mid-market manufacturing company alive in Italy's tough economy. Every day felt like survival—competing with giants, watching smaller firms collapse around me. Then came the announcement: the China-Italy Industrial Cooperation Fund. 600 million euros. A partnership between UniCredit, Investindustrial, and China's Investment Corporation. My hands trembled reading the details. This fund was designed for companies like mine—Italian businesses desperate to expand beyond our saturated home market. China represented possibility, a vast consumer base hungry for European quality and innovation. I attended the investor meetings, listening as Andrea Bonomi spoke of doubling their China-focused team, as Richard Burton promised to accelerate our international growth. The CIC representatives outlined their vision: advanced manufacturing, consumer goods, healthcare sectors—exactly where my company operated. For the first time in years, I felt hope. This wasn't charity; it was strategic partnership. Chinese consumers would finally access our products. My employees might keep their jobs. My business might not just survive—it could thrive. The fund represented my second chance at success.

Y [2014-10], As a rescuer looking over a wounded Iraq, I hear Mar Louis Raphael I Sako speak like a hand reaching into the smoke. From Baghdad, he sends Eid al-Adha greetings to Muslims and asks God to protect the country from every evil. His words do not hide the damage: war, displacement, fear, and the crushing weight of violent extremism that has torn communities apart. He calls for rescue through honesty, education, and reconciliation. He urges Iraqis to recognize one another as brothers and partners in one land, and to rebuild trust through dialogue, tolerance, justice, and respect for religious and cultural differences. In his voice, I hear a roadmap for saving what remains of national unity. He also speaks for Christians who have been driven from their towns by ISIS and pressured even in Baghdad, yet still refuse hatred. They remain, he says, committed to loving everyone, including Muslims who reject violence and stand with the innocent, like Dr. Mohammed Al-Asali, who died defending Christians in Mosul. The patriarch appeals to the national government and the Kurdistan Regional Government to work together quickly to liberate Mosul and the Nineveh Plain, so displaced families can return home before winter and schools reopen. His message is a rescue call: save people, not sacrifice them.

Y [2019-07], My grandfather always told me that justice is a cold, unyielding machine, and watching the news from July 2019, I finally understood what he meant.
