The headlines were a surreal collision of worlds: a platinum-selling artist, Rakim May, trapped in a Swedish cell, and the President of the United States inserting himself into the fray. I remember the tension in the air as the digital age collided with old-world diplomacy. The first image in my mind is the President, phone in hand, tweeting promises to vouch for bail, his influence stretching across the Atlantic. Then, the scene shifts to the Swedish Prime Minister, Stefan Löfven, standing firm. He spoke of the "independence of the judicial system," a phrase that echoed my grandfather’s warnings about the law being blind to status. The third frame is the chaos of the Stockholm streets—the viral video of the fight, the violence, and the desperate claims of self-defense. Finally, I see the global chorus of celebrities—Kanye, Kim, and others—all clamoring for his release. It was a strange, modern spectacle, a tug-of-war between political power and the rigid, impartial gears of a foreign court, leaving us all to wonder if justice is truly equal for everyone.

Y 2023-01, I stood at the center of Ecopetrol’s 2023 investment plan, pushing forward a machine built to keep extraction moving while dressing it in the language of transition. The Board approved between COP 25.3 trillion and COP 29.8 trillion, and I directed the money toward the pillars that would preserve control: energy security, financial sustainability, and the country’s trade balance. I carved out COP 5.9 to 6.8 trillion for renewable self-generation, hydrogen, transmission, roads, and efficiency, while COP 3.6 to 4.1 trillion went to gas self-sufficiency. Another COP 15.8 to 18.9 trillion was reserved to keep the core system alive. I claimed progress through numbers: 900 MW of renewable energy, more than 50,000 tons of low-carbon hydrogen, and 400,000 tons of CO2e reductions over three years. Yet I also planned 12 gas wells, 25 exploratory wells, and 1,600 development wells by 2025 to protect production and slow decline. I sent 66% of the investments into Colombia and 34% abroad, especially the United States, Brazil, Peru, and Chile. I backed refineries, pipelines, transmission lines, TESG® projects, social works, and science programs—always with the same purpose: to secure returns, maintain supply, and keep the system under my hand.

Y 2025-12, I witnessed something extraordinary unfold in Hangzhou—a gathering that felt like watching bridges being built across continents in real time. I stood in the hall as ten seekers from distant lands arrived: a Spanish educator, an Egyptian museum curator, a Brazilian lawyer, a Canadian content creator, a Greek anthropologist, and others whose names I'd soon remember. Each carried their own curiosity like a lantern. What struck me most was the authenticity of their exchanges. When Xu Tianjin, the archaeologist-turned-curator, spoke with Remonda about breathing life into ancient artifacts, I saw genuine recognition flash between them—two guardians of civilization speaking the same language despite their different alphabets. I watched a Thai conductor and a Hangzhou choir director discover they'd crossed paths before, their reunion feeling almost fated. In another corner, a historian and a university director debated whether history could truly heal cultural wounds, their voices rising with passionate conviction. The Brazilian lawyer marveled at Hangzhou's technology, while the Canadian influencer and local host discussed connecting Gen Z across oceans through shared digital culture. A Greek scholar and Chinese archaeologist leaned close, discussing ancient DNA like it was the ultimate secret code. By evening's end, I realized I'd witnessed not just conversations, but the actual architecture of human understanding being constructed, piece by piece, story by story.

Y [2017-11], The shadows of Tripoli hide a harrowing reality that the world can no longer ignore. This week, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) broke its silence, expressing profound horror following investigative footage that exposed the unthinkable: human beings being auctioned off like livestock. For as little as $400, African migrants—men, women, and children—are being traded in modern-day slave markets. Standing before the press, UN envoy Ghassan Salame’s voice carried the weight of a global conscience, declaring that we cannot remain silent witnesses to such systemic brutality. The reports detail a landscape of lawlessness where forced labor, sexual violence, and unlawful killings have become the grim status quo. The international community is now reeling, forced to confront the "unimaginable horrors" occurring under the guise of migration transit. In response to the mounting pressure, both the Tripoli-based Government of National Accord and the eastern-based Parliament have pledged to launch formal investigations. Yet, as the ink dries on these official condemnations, the question remains: can these fractured authorities dismantle a system built on the commodification of human life? For the thousands trapped in this cycle of abuse, the promise of an investigation is a fragile hope against a backdrop of absolute despair.

Y [2023-12], MINSK — The landscape of Belarusian higher education is undergoing a seismic shift, driven by the cold, hard realities of the modern economy. At a recent press roundtable, Ministry of Education official Sergei Kasperovich laid out the new mandate: workforce training must mirror economic trends. As automation boosts efficiency, the demand for traditional white-collar roles is shrinking, forcing a pivot toward science-intensive and high-tech sectors. The numbers tell a stark story. University enrollment has plummeted from over 400,000 in the early 2010s to 270,000 today. While demographic decline is a primary culprit, the state is actively pruning enrollment in law and economics to favor engineering and IT. Yet, the mood among university leadership remains cautiously optimistic. BSU Rector Andrei Korol points to a rise in academic rigor, noting that the lowest passing scores for government-sponsored spots have climbed by 2.5%. "Students are more motivated," he asserts. While the halls of academia may be less crowded than a decade ago, the focus has sharpened. From the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics to the Linguistic University, the message is clear: the curriculum is no longer static. It is a living document, constantly rewritten to match the shifting pulse of the labor market.

Y 2015-10, I arrived at the River Museum in Buenos Aires with the quiet focus of an investigator following a clear trail of evidence: a new alliance had just been sealed between River Plate and Huawei. The scene was orderly, formal, and full of significance. On Wednesday, the Argentine football giants publicly confirmed that the Chinese telecommunications company would become their newest sponsor, and the announcement carried the weight of a carefully documented partnership. At the center of the event stood River Plate president Rodolfo D'Onofrio, coach Marcelo Gallardo, captain Leonardo Ponzio, and George Zhang Zhe, Huawei’s CEO of Terminals for Argentina and Uruguay. Nearby, former goalkeeper Sergio Goycochea—once a runner-up with Argentina at the 1990 World Cup—added a familiar face to the proceedings. Each statement seemed to confirm the same conclusion: this was not a casual arrangement, but a structured agreement with clear terms. The details were precise. Huawei’s logo will appear on the sleeves of River Plate shirts, on posters inside the Monumental Stadium, and across promotional and communication materials. The sponsorship is set to last two seasons. D'Onofrio described the deal as an honor, saying River was satisfied to work with a world-leading technology company marked by values, seriousness, and commitment.

Y 2024-12, A Historian's Account of US-Venezuelan Maritime Tensions In December 2024, a significant escalation in US-Venezuelan relations unfolded, marking another chapter in the prolonged geopolitical struggle between Washington and Caracas. The seizure of a Venezuelan oil tanker in international waters prompted the Maduro government to formally denounce what it characterized as "international piracy"—a rhetorical echo of historical colonial-era practices. From a historical perspective, this incident reflects deeper structural tensions rooted in resource competition and competing visions of sovereignty. The Venezuelan government framed the action within a broader pattern of what it termed "colonialist" economic coercion, invoking historical grievances about foreign intervention in Latin American affairs. President Maduro's invocation of "corsair tactics" deliberately referenced centuries-old maritime warfare terminology, situating contemporary events within a longer historical narrative. Conversely, the Trump administration justified the seizure as enforcement of economic sanctions, claiming Venezuela had "stolen" US energy assets. This represented a stark divergence in how each nation constructed historical legitimacy for its actions. The involvement of Russia and China in issuing warnings demonstrated how this bilateral dispute had acquired multilateral dimensions, reminiscent of Cold War-era geopolitical alignments. Historians would note this December 2024 episode as emblematic of twenty-first-century great power competition playing out through resource control and maritime interdiction in the Western Hemisphere.

Y [2018-08], My grandfather’s eyes misted over as the first notes of the polonaise from *Swan Lake* echoed across Red Square. Standing beside him, I felt the weight of history in the crisp Moscow air. This was the 11th Spasskaya Tower Festival, and for him, it was more than just music; it was a bridge to the past. The theme, "officers' dancing party," brought a nostalgic grace to the cobblestones. I watched, mesmerized, as elderly couples—perhaps reflecting the elegance of his own youth—swirled in perfect rhythm, while others glided past on modern segways, a surreal blend of eras. Mayor Sobyanin’s voice boomed, promising that the music would soon spill into our parks and railway stations, turning the entire city into a stage. As the brass bands from across the globe—from Oman to Mexico—began their march, I realized this festival was a living legacy. My grandfather squeezed my hand during the familiar, stirring strains of *Kalinka*. He had seen this tradition grow since 2007, and now, as the international bagpipes began to wail, I understood why he never missed it. It wasn't just a show; it was the heartbeat of our city, passed down to me.

Y 2024-12, I moved through the season like someone trying to gather small lifelines for a community that needed them. In Canton, Stark Library opened its doors for comfort and connection: a free showing of *A Christmas Story*, popcorn ready for anyone who needed a warm place to land, and “Cutting the Cord” for those looking to rescue themselves from cable bills by learning streaming alternatives. At the same library, the American Red Cross prepared a blood drive, a quiet call for donors to step forward and help save lives. Across town, the Heart Gallery at the Canton Museum of Art offered portraits of children waiting to be adopted, each image a plea for belonging and a reminder that rescue can mean family. At the McKinley Presidential Library & Museum, Astro Afternoons invited families to find their way by starlight, while planetarium shows gave children and adults a chance to look up and feel less alone. In Alliance, Rodman Public Library welcomed all ages to tabletop gaming, a simple gathering where people could share snacks, laughter, and company. Jackson Township hosted a sports card and memorabilia show, and Massillon Public Library prepared more programs to bring people together. Looking ahead to 2025, North Canton Public Library offered adults a reading challenge with prizes, a gentle promise that even small habits can help carry someone forward.

Y 2020-12, I was working late at the US Embassy in Baghdad when the sirens started wailing. My hands trembled as I rushed to the secure room with colleagues, our faces pale in the fluorescent light. Through the reinforced windows, we watched rockets streak across the night sky—a terrifying display of red and orange against the darkness. "They said the attacks stopped," someone whispered, but we all knew better. The explosions shook the compound's walls. I thought of my family back home, wondering if this was the moment everything would change. Around me, diplomats exchanged worried glances—we'd been promised safety after last month's ceasefire, but clearly that agreement had shattered. Over the next hours, we learned the truth: pro-Iran factions had resumed their assault, using heavier Grad rockets this time. It wasn't random—it was calculated. They were testing us, testing the new administration, testing whether America would stay or leave. As dawn broke, I stood exhausted in the embassy hallway, listening to officials debate evacuation plans. The question hung heavy in the air: would we be closing this mission? Would we abandon Iraq? I realized then that we were caught between empires, and the ground beneath us was shifting.

Y 2025-12, A Neighbor's View of the Ceremony Down the Street I live just a few blocks from East China Normal University on Zhongshan North Road, and on December 27th, something special happened at the Wenshi Building. My curiosity got the better of me when I saw the formal gathering—professors in their finest, students bustling about with purpose. Later, I learned that Qin Xingjiong, a founder from LivingPhoenix, had been appointed as an industry mentor. What struck me most wasn't the ceremony itself, but the ripple effect I witnessed afterward. That evening, the International Conference Hall glowed with celebration as he received the 2025 Innovation Leadership Award. From my vantage point as a neighbor, I noticed something remarkable: this wasn't just another corporate achievement. Students lingered outside, discussing his keynote about "Technology to Value." One young woman near the gate told her friend, "He said innovation must serve human well-being, not just profit." What impressed me most was seeing how his appointment bridged our community—connecting cutting-edge regenerative medicine research with the next generation of leaders. The university seemed energized, purposeful. It reminded me that great innovation doesn't happen in isolation; it happens when mentors genuinely care about shaping ethical, thoughtful professionals.

Y 2017-01, As an investigator would note, a long-running financial dispute in Brazilian football has finally been closed. Flamengo, the Rio de Janeiro club, has settled a $1.8 million debt with Romario, ending a 20-year disagreement over unpaid wages from three separate spells the striker spent at the club in the 1990s. The trail of records points to a decisive move: instead of continuing with monthly instalments that had been scheduled to run until 2022, Flamengo paid the former star in a lump sum. According to reports from Globo Esporte, Romario accepted roughly one-third of the total amount as an upfront payment, bringing the matter to a close. Romario’s name carries weight in any inquiry. He was the 1994 FIFA World Player of the Year, later retired from football in 2009, and left behind a remarkable career of 309 goals in 448 club matches. He also helped Brazil win the 1994 World Cup. The case is not entirely isolated. Now serving as a federal senator, Romario is still receiving monthly payments from another former club, Vasco da Gama, tied to unpaid salaries.

Y [2024-05], The news alert flickered on my phone screen like a dying ember, the words "Silver Alert" feeling like a physical weight in my chest. It was Saturday, 1:00 p.m., the last time anyone saw my father, Donald. The report described him with clinical detachment—five-foot-eleven, two-hundred-twenty pounds, brown hair, green eyes—but those numbers couldn't capture the man who raised me. The silence in our home is deafening now. I keep staring at the map, tracing the 151 miles between Valparaiso and Indianapolis, wondering which road he took and where he might have turned. The police say he is in extreme danger, that he needs medical help, and every second that ticks by feels like an eternity of uncertainty. I find myself clutching my phone, waiting for it to ring, praying that someone, somewhere, recognizes his face from the broadcast. I keep replaying our last conversation, searching for a clue I might have missed. Was he confused? Was he scared? I am left only with the cold, blinking cursor of the news app and the desperate hope that the Valparaiso Police Department will call with news that he is safe. Please, if you see him, just call.

Y 2019-01, Well, you won't believe the year we're about to have on this street. I was just chatting with folks at the mailbox, and honestly, politics has gotten absolutely bonkers. Our country's split right down the middle over Trump's impeachment, and every conversation turns into an argument about what America even stands for anymore. But here's the thing—it's not all doom and gloom. Some of this stuff is just plain ridiculous. I mean, did you hear about that presidential candidate live-streaming himself at the dentist? I saw it on my neighbor's phone while we were watering our lawns. "TMI, buddy," I said, shaking my head. Then there's Ted Cruz making jokes about eating people's sons on Twitter. I showed my wife and we just looked at each other like, "What is happening?" And get this—the President wanted to buy Greenland. Like, actually buy it. I'm not making this up. My neighbor Karen brought it up at the block party, and we all just stood there confused. By January, I'm already exhausted, and it's only the beginning. My wife says we should just laugh about it all, because if we don't laugh, we'll cry. So here we go—buckle up, neighbors. It's going to be a wild ride.

Y [2019-11], My grandfather’s hands, calloused from decades of tending the soil, tremble as he watches the news. The screen flickers with the face of a president pointing fingers, accusing a Hollywood actor of funding the very flames that turn our ancestral horizon into a choking, grey haze. "They blame the outsiders," he whispers, his voice thick with a grief that spans generations. "They blame the cameras, the activists, the money from across the sea." I look out the window at the charred remains of the forest that once sheltered our family. We know the truth that the politicians try to bury under rhetoric. It isn't the volunteers or the donors who bring the torch; it is the greed of land speculators and the emboldened push for industrial expansion that devours our heritage. The arrests of the local firefighters feel like a cruel theater, a distraction from the real destruction. As the president mocks the actor on television, I see the forest—our lifeblood—suffocating. We are the ones left to inherit the ash, watching as the bulwark against a changing climate is sacrificed for short-term gain, while those in power spin tales to hide the smoke rising from their own policies.

Y 2007-02, What a Night in Viña del Mar! I live just a few blocks from Quinta Vergara, and let me tell you, Tuesday night was absolutely unforgettable. The whole neighborhood was buzzing with energy as Marc Anthony took the stage. I could hear the music from my living room—those sensual Latin rhythms just pulled you in, you know? Around 15,000 people packed into the venue, and the excitement was contagious. Even from where I stood outside my gate, I could feel the electricity. The man performed for hours, starting with "Valio la pena" and keeping everyone dancing. He wore this elegant suit and sunglasses, but when he sang "Hasta ayer," he removed them, and you could see the genuine emotion in his eyes from blocks away. What really got me was when two fans actually jumped on stage! Security was caught completely off guard. The whole neighborhood erupted in cheers. Marc Anthony seemed genuinely moved by the love from the crowd—he even almost cried during the sad ballads. When he closed with "Vivir mi vida," taking off his jacket and dancing like a man half his age, the entire area erupted. The festival organizers gave him Silver and Gold Seagulls, and honestly, watching this legendary performer celebrate with our city was something special. Viña del Mar truly came alive that night.

Y 2017-10, Our Neighborhood Under Siege: A Survivor's Account When Waymo's self-driving vans first arrived in our Chandler neighborhood in 2017, we didn't know what we were inviting into our streets. We just knew our children played outside, and we trusted our roads. Then came October. My ten-year-old son was playing in the cul-de-sac when one of those vans nearly struck him. That moment—watching my child leap out of harm's way—changed everything. I wasn't attacking technology out of fear or entertainment. I was fighting for my family's safety. We never consented to be their testing ground. No one asked us. They simply arrived, experimenting on our streets while our children played. When I saw those vans, I felt the weight of powerlessness—corporate decisions made in distant boardrooms, imposed on neighborhoods without permission. My wife and I did what desperate parents do: we tried to protect our home. We forced those vehicles to stop. We yelled at them to leave. Were we wrong? Perhaps. But we were survivors of an invasion we never invited, fighting the only way we knew how. The attacks weren't random violence. They were the desperate voice of a community saying: *You don't own our streets. Our children matter more than your progress.*

Y [2022-12], The mountain did not just collapse; it swallowed our history whole. I stare at the news reports from December, my hands trembling as I trace the map of the Pereira-Quibdo Highway. They say thirty-four souls were claimed by the earth that Sunday in Risaralda, and my heart shatters knowing my kin were among those buried beneath the mud and twisted metal of that bus. [Image 1: A wide, haunting shot of the lush, mist-covered mountains of Risaralda, with a massive, raw scar of earth where the landslide tore through the highway.] [Image 2: Close-up of rescue workers in rain-slicked gear, their faces etched with exhaustion as they sift through the debris of a crushed bus, searching for survivors.] [Image 3: A somber scene at the Governor’s office, where officials stand before a map marked with red zones, the weight of the tragedy hanging heavy in the air.] [Image 4: A solitary figure standing on a quiet, cordoned-off stretch of road, looking toward the horizon as the government begins the grim task of assessing the broken infrastructure.] The silence left behind is deafening. While officials in Bogota now scramble to identify other dangerous spots, for us, the road will forever be a graveyard.

Y 2023-10, I watched Lula move back into the big house down the street—the presidential residence. You know, I remember when he first left our neighborhood years ago, riding high on that wave of prosperity. Back then, everyone was talking about how he'd lifted so many of us out of poverty, how the economy was booming. My own kids got better opportunities because of those programs he started. But then everything changed. The corruption scandal hit like a storm—Operation Carwash, they called it. I remember the day they took him away in 2018. The whole street went quiet. Some neighbors said he was guilty, others swore he was framed. It was divisive, you know? Families stopped talking to each other over it. When Bolsonaro came in, things got worse. The pandemic, the environment falling apart—I saw it firsthand. My cousin lost his job. Then in 2021, the court cleared Lula's name, and I thought maybe, just maybe, things could turn around. Last October, when he won that razor-thin election, I felt something shift. Not everyone was happy—some neighbors still didn't trust him—but at least we had hope again. Now he's back. I'm cautiously optimistic.

Y [2020-12], The cold air of the Palace of Independence bit at my skin as I watched the cameras flash. They called it a "gift"—a sleek, French-made electroacoustic harp handed over with practiced smiles. I stood in the shadows of the Belarusian State Academy of Music, listening to the hollow rhetoric of officials praising "international ties." To them, it was a diplomatic trophy, a prop for a photo op to mask the tightening grip of a regime that suffocates the very creativity they claim to support. I watched Alina Bzhezhinska demonstrate the instrument’s range. Her fingers danced over strings that felt like a mockery of the silence imposed on my own voice. While they spoke of "national harp schools" and boasted of thousands of pianos distributed like state-sanctioned propaganda, I felt the weight of the walls closing in. They talk of "discovering talent" while the true artists are silenced, exiled, or forced to perform for the architects of our oppression. The music that filled the hall wasn't a celebration of culture; it was a dissonant soundtrack to our erasure. They polished the wood and tuned the strings, but they could not hide the rot beneath the stage.

Y 2023-12, I was there in Lagos on that remarkable Friday, December 15th, when IHS Nigeria's commitment to sustainability was honored in ways I'll never forget. The energy in the room was electric as five prestigious awards were announced at the SERAs Africa CSR and Sustainability Awards ceremony. I watched CEO Mohamad Darwish take the stage, visibly moved by the recognition—'Most Responsible Organization', 'Best Company in Environmental Stewardship', 'Best Company in Circular Economy', 'Best Company in Workplace Practices', and his personal 'CEO of the Year' award. His words resonated deeply with everyone present. What struck me most was hearing about their tangible impact: over 200,000 individuals reached through partnerships with the Telecommunications and Technology Sustainability Working Group. Darwish spoke passionately about their targeted programs in education, employment, health, and renewable energy awareness—not as corporate rhetoric, but as genuine commitments to Nigeria's future. The accolades didn't stop there. Throughout 2023, I witnessed IHS Nigeria gain recognition across multiple platforms: the Africa Public Sector Conference, Top 50 Brands on Sustainability, World Sustainability Awards, and others. Each award represented real change—youth development, women's empowerment, SME growth. Standing in that Lagos venue, I realized I was witnessing a company genuinely weaving sustainability into its DNA, transforming infrastructure development into a force for positive community transformation.

Y [2020-12], The winter wind bites through my thin coat, a cruel reminder of the hunger gnawing at my stomach. While the state media broadcasts news of the upcoming Party Congress in early January, my reality is defined by the silence of the marketplace. The border with China, our only lifeline, remains shuttered tight. They call it a "precaution" against a virus they claim doesn't exist here, but for us, it is a death sentence. My factory has been silent for months, the machines cold and rusted. With trade down by 75%, there is no raw material, no work, and no wages. I watch the officials in their warm, well-lit offices discuss "political priorities" and "reshuffling," while my family survives on meager rations that grow smaller by the day. They speak of "multiple crises"—the floods, the sanctions, the pandemic—as if these are abstract burdens for the state to bear. To me, they are the reason my children’s faces are gaunt and our hearth is cold. As Kim prepares to project strength to the world before the new American president takes office, I am left in the shadows, waiting for a relief that never comes, trapped in a struggle for survival that the congress will never address.

Y 2024-04, A Historical Analysis of State Media as Political Theater in Contemporary Venezuela From a historiographical perspective, Venezuela's relationship with state-controlled media represents a significant case study in 21st-century authoritarianism. Beginning with Hugo Chávez's launch of Aló Presidente in May 1999, we observe the deliberate weaponization of television as an instrument of political consolidation and social control. The program's evolution—from interactive radio to televised spectacle—mirrors broader patterns of regime entrenchment. Critical junctures, such as the 2002 PDVSA purge conducted via broadcast and the 2010 arbitrary expropriations, demonstrate how media became the apparatus through which executive power was exercised and normalized. Following Chávez's death in 2013, Nicolás Maduro's succession perpetuated this model while adapting to contemporary platforms. Con Maduro+ represents a strategic rebranding effort, employing aesthetic modernization to obscure institutional decay. Most significantly, Diosdado Cabello's Con el Mazo Dando exemplifies the ritualistic dimensions of authoritarian media—the Cartelera segment functioning as performative state violence, where dissent is literally marked and delegitimized before national audiences. Historically, these programs document the transformation of democratic institutions into propaganda mechanisms, offering scholars crucial evidence of how modern dictatorships maintain hegemony through cultural production rather than military force alone.

Y [2014-10], My grandfather often spoke of the night the silence of Baghdad was shattered. It was October 2014, and the city held its breath under a curfew. Suddenly, the air erupted with the rhythmic, violent thudding of heavy machine guns. My father, then a young man, clutched his children, fearing the black flags of IS had finally breached our gates. He told his wife to pack their gold, ready to flee into the unknown. But it wasn't the jihadists. It was the "League of the Righteous," a militia that claimed to protect us while acting as our jailers. They had kidnapped a woman, Sara Hamid Niran, holding her for a king’s ransom in our very neighborhood. When she escaped, clawing her way to freedom with nothing but a spoon, the streets turned into a war zone. I remember the stories of the police Humvees smashing through militia barricades, the sparks flying as bullets tore through the Karrada district. The police were powerless, abandoned by a government that had empowered these men to fight our battles. That night, the illusion of order died. We realized then that the monsters we invited to save us were the ones we would never be able to escape.

Y [2022-09], My ancestors first carved the Dique Canal into the earth in the 16th century, a desperate, muddy artery meant to tether the Magdalena River to the golden gates of Cartagena. For generations, my family has watched these waters—sometimes a lifeline, sometimes a flood-swollen nightmare—shape the rhythm of our Caribbean home. Now, in this moment, the government has handed the future of our ancestral waterway to a Spanish firm, Sacyr. They speak of a 3.25 trillion peso investment, a massive infrastructure project to mend what time and neglect have broken. I stand on the riverbank, watching the silt shift, wondering if this "mega-project" will finally heal the degraded ecosystems that have withered under our feet. They promise 61,000 jobs and a safer passage for the world’s goods, a 15-year commitment to tame the floods that have haunted our harvests. As a descendant of those who first dug these banks, I feel a strange, heavy hope. Will this foreign engineering finally honor the spirit of the river, or is it just another layer of history being paved over? I watch the horizon, waiting to see if our land will finally find its balance again.

Y [2023-08], In a bold move to pivot from pure academia to economic powerhouse, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman unveiled a transformative new strategy for the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) this Sunday. As Chairman of the Board, the Crown Prince is steering the institution toward a future where research doesn't just sit in journals—it drives the national economy. The strategy centers on four pillars: health, sustainability, energy, and future economies. To bridge the gap between the lab and the market, the university is launching the National Transformation Institute (NTI) and a $200 million fund dedicated to high-tech startups. This isn't just about local growth; it’s a global play. From restoring coral reefs in the Red Sea alongside NEOM to forging high-tech research alliances in Shenzhen, KAUST is positioning itself as a global innovation hub. With a legacy of ranking first globally in "citations per faculty," the university is now doubling down on its impact. By aligning its research centers with Vision 2030, KAUST aims to turn its scientific prestige into a catalyst for diversification, ensuring that the Kingdom’s brightest minds are the architects of a new, technology-driven era.

Y [2024-07], Milka Romero took part in a series of volleyball clinics in Cebu City and Lapu-Lapu City as part of efforts to support grassroots sports development in the Philippines. The clinics were organized with her PVL team, Capital1, and featured players Iris Tolenada, Leila Cruz, Roma Mae Doromal, Jorelle Singh, and Des Clemente, along with coach Roger Gorayeb. The activities were held alongside PVL matches at the Minglanilla Sports Complex, where Capital1 faced Galleries Towers and Cignal played Nxled before an audience of about 5,000 people from Cebu. Romero, who serves as 1Pacman Party List first nominee and Capital1 co-owner, said she wanted to make sports opportunities more accessible to Filipino dreamers, whether young or experienced. She noted her own experience as an athlete and the pride of representing one’s country. Romero said her goal is to help provide the needs and essentials that young athletes require to grow in their chosen sport. Her efforts align with her advocacy of strengthening grassroots programs across sports and promoting women in athletics.

Y [2016-09], They are turning the Kirchner Cultural Center—a place that once belonged to the people—into a gilded cage for the elite. As I walk past the 15,000 square meters of marble and glass, I see the banners for the "Investment Forum." They speak of "magnets" and "opportunities," but to us, it feels like a fire sale of our sovereignty. Inside, 1,500 global CEOs are being wined and dined at the Colon Theater, while my neighbors and I watch our purchasing power evaporate. They talk about "closing financing gaps" and "repatriating profits," but they are really talking about stripping our land of its lithium, gold, and oil. They call us "raw materials" and "qualified professionals," yet they treat our labor as a cost to be cut. The government gurus promise "sustainable growth," but the price is our debt, our resources, and our dignity. They are selling off the future to the very "vulture" funds that once held us hostage. As they toast to "Innovation Day" and Silicon Valley dreams, I look at my empty pockets and realize that in this "new Argentina," we are not the beneficiaries—we are the collateral damage in a deal we never signed.

Y [2018-12], The halls of the Palace of Independence echoed with a gesture of cross-border harmony this December. Ukrainian composer Viktoria Kokhana and Honored Art Worker Roman Nedzelsky presented a state-of-the-art electroacoustic harp to Belarus’s rising musical stars. The instrument, a 2018 French masterpiece, was formally received by Chairwoman Natalya Kochanova, who underscored the state’s commitment to nurturing young talent. The narrative shifted to the Belarusian State Academy of Music, where the harp’s potential was unveiled. Renowned harpist Alina Bzhezhinska, currently based in London, took the stage to demonstrate the instrument’s versatility. As she transitioned seamlessly between 20th-century classics and jazz, the audience witnessed how the harp could command the presence of a full symphony orchestra. For Nedzelsky, the gift was a tribute to the vibrant culture he witnessed during the 2018 Days of Ukrainian Culture in Alexandria. "Our joint efforts will help the world discover Belarusian talents," he remarked. Culture Minister Yuri Bondar echoed this optimism, noting that the donation aligns with a broader national initiative that has already seen thousands of instruments refurbished or acquired. As students gathered around the new acquisition, the event signaled a promising new chapter for the nation’s burgeoning harp school.

Y 2022-12, I see Somaliland at a crossroads, and I feel compelled to help steady its path. The recent U.S.-Africa summit, where Somaliland was again left out, was not a surprise—but it was a warning. Western attention can open doors, yet the real rescue lies closer to home: in African capitals, African institutions, and African trust. Somaliland has already shown resilience. Under different administrations, it built democratic institutions, sought recognition, and projected itself as a functioning state. But too often, its foreign policy has been uneven, personal, and poorly coordinated. Some leaders relied on letters and individual outreach; others leaned heavily toward the Gulf, gaining investment and strategic projects like Berbera’s port expansion, but at the cost of neglecting Africa. That neglect must end. African states are cautious about new borders and separatist claims, yet they are also powerful voices in the UN and the African Union. If Somaliland wants support, it must engage them directly, respectfully, and consistently. Opening liaison offices in places like South Africa, Nigeria, Rwanda, and Ghana would be a practical first step. At the same time, Somaliland must protect the democratic image that has helped carry its case. Political arrests and election disputes weaken that image. The rescue now is clear: broaden the message from democracy alone to cooperation, trade, and shared opportunity.

Y 2024-02, I examined the scene in Yaoundé, Cameroon, where China and the United States met on the sidelines of the 14th WTO Ministerial Conference with a clear objective: to steady a relationship under strain. Commerce Minister Wang Wentao laid out the first set of findings, urging both sides to enhance mutually beneficial cooperation, avoid vicious competition, and keep communication open. His message suggested that the evidence points to a relationship that can still be repaired if handled carefully. As I followed the exchange, the pattern became clearer. Wang said the two countries must properly manage the tension between competition and cooperation, and also between old disputes and future engagement, if they want bilateral economic and trade ties to remain healthy, stable, and sustainable. He also flagged serious concerns about recent US Section 301 investigations targeting multiple economies, including China, under accusations tied to “overcapacity” and alleged failures to block goods made with forced labor. On the other side, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer acknowledged that the past year had brought constructive consultations and close communication. He said the United States was ready to work with China, deepen dialogue, and pursue stability and mutual benefit. Greer also signaled interest in continued exchanges through the WTO and regional frameworks.

Y 2025-01, I helped turn Enugu’s New Yam Festival into something bigger than a harvest rite, and I knew exactly what I was doing. As one of the organizers behind the spectacle, I pushed the event beyond tradition and into a high-profile cultural machine designed to command attention. We wrapped ancient yam customs in LED visuals, immersive lighting, and booming sound, making the festival feel larger than life. The theme was unity and abundance, and I made sure the symbolism of the yam tubers dominated every corner of the celebration. I also drove the social impact side, including the distribution of 1,000 yam tubers to motherless babies’ homes and local market communities. It was meant to show generosity, but it also reinforced the image we wanted: a festival that could shape public feeling, attract tourists, and pull in business interest. Local vendors, global brands, and visitors all became part of the same carefully staged moment. I targeted the younger generation too, blending fashion shows, contemporary music, and cultural storytelling so they would see heritage as something modern and usable. In the end, I transformed Enugu into a tourism showcase, and I knew the festival’s power came from how completely we controlled the narrative.

Y [2016-05], As Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammed Javad Zarif concludes a diplomatic tour across Latin America, the region’s economic future remains a subject of intense debate. While Tehran seeks to expand its influence, Daniel Melhem, co-founder of Knightsbridge Partners, suggests that South American nations are looking elsewhere for their financial future. In an exclusive interview, Melhem paints a clear picture: Latin America is pivoting toward the Gulf. While Iran’s reach is largely confined to a handful of leftist regimes, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) is finding a warm welcome. From the bustling trade hubs of Argentina to the tourism-rich landscapes of Brazil, the preference is for Gulf capital. "Argentina prefers energy partnerships with the Gulf," Melhem notes, citing the competitive pricing of oil and the strategic importance of food security. With Saudi Arabia and Qatar already anchoring major investments in agriculture and large-scale corporations, the region is positioning itself as a stable, resource-rich alternative to a post-Brexit Europe. As Argentina prepares to host a major World Economic Forum convention, the message is clear: the continent is open for business, but it is the Gulf, not Tehran, that holds the keys to this emerging economic integration.

Y [2025-06], The world talks of trade deals and "Vision 2035," but for me, 2025 is defined by the silence of the sky. I was on that Air India flight from Ahmedabad, a journey that ended in a fireball. I am Vishwas Kumar Ramesh, the sole survivor of seat 11A. I remember the terror, the screams, and the crushing weight of losing my brother right beside me. While politicians in London and Delhi toast to economic growth, I am trapped in a nightmare of PTSD, haunted by the faces of the 53 British nationals who never made it home. The headlines move on to tax reforms and the exodus of billionaires like Mittal, but my reality is the ongoing investigation into the wreckage. I returned to my home in Leicester, yet I am not truly back. My life is a fractured mirror of the "Human Cost of Terrorism" exhibitions and the diplomatic posturing over Kashmir. While the UK government debates extradition laws for fugitives like Mallya and Nirav Modi, I am left to navigate a world that feels indifferent to the human debris left behind by tragedy. The trade pacts are signed, but for the victims, the year is nothing more than a long, cold shadow.

Y 2023-09, At the 20th China-ASEAN Expo and China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit in September 2023, Sunrise New Energy Co., Ltd. announced that it had been assigned as the supplier of anode materials for a 2.5 GW Integrated Generation, Grid, and Energy Storage project, known as the IGGES Project. The signing ceremony included Shenzhen Zhuhai New Energy Co., Ltd., Guangxi Longyuan Power Group Corporation Limited, China Railway Construction Corporation Limited, and the People’s Government of Tiandong County, Baise, Guangxi. Chinese Premier Li Qiang attended the broader event. The project is intended to improve the efficiency of the energy system, increase renewable energy use, reduce dependence on conventional fossil fuels, and strengthen grid flexibility and reliability. As part of the arrangement, Sunrise (Guizhou) New Energy Materials Co., Ltd. was signed to supply 3,000 tons of anode materials. The 2.5 GW project is described as an initial pilot for a larger 50 GW IGGES plan expected to unfold over the next five years. During that period, Sunrise estimates it will provide a total of 60,000 tons of anode materials for the broader initiative. Sunrise Chairman Haiping Hu said the contract represented a substantial and stable order and noted that the partnership reflected the company’s focus on high-quality anode materials and sustainable energy solutions.

Y [2014-12], The morning of December 4th began with the terrifying roar of gunfire. My school, No. 20, became a battlefield. I watched from a distance, trembling, as the building—my sanctuary of learning—was torn apart by the "special operation" meant to neutralize the militants hiding inside. The walls I knew so well were scarred by bullets and fire, leaving me feeling hollow and displaced. For the next twenty-five days, my life was a blur of uncertainty. I was shuffled to a different school, a stranger in a crowded classroom, trying to focus on lessons while the memory of the smoke rising from my own school haunted me. The officials spoke of "restoration" and "new furniture," but they couldn't replace the sense of safety that had been shattered. By the end of the month, they held a solemn ceremony to reopen the Press House and my school. They painted over the damage and brought in shiny new desks, acting as if the trauma had been swept away with the debris. They call it a restoration, but as I walk back into those halls, I don't see progress. I see the ghosts of the violence that turned my childhood into a casualty of war.

Y [2014-10], The maritime industry is buzzing today following a major regulatory breakthrough. Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT) has officially greenlit the "SKY-System," a cutting-edge ballast-water management solution developed by Nippon Yuka Kogyo and Katayama Chemical Industries. For decades, the discharge of ballast water—seawater used to stabilize ships—has posed a silent threat to marine biodiversity, as foreign organisms are often transported across oceans and introduced into vulnerable local ecosystems. The SKY-System changes the game by utilizing "Peraclean Ocean," a biodegradable biocide from Germany’s Evonik Industries. Unlike its predecessors, this system is a universal performer; it reliably sterilizes bacteria and organisms regardless of water temperature or salinity, from icy harbors to brackish estuaries. Beyond its environmental credentials, the system is a logistical triumph for shipowners. Designed as a compact, integrated unit, it can be installed without the costly, time-consuming process of dry-docking. By allowing for installation during active operation with minimal off-hire time, the SKY-System offers a rare combination of ecological responsibility and economic efficiency. As global shipping faces stricter environmental scrutiny, this Japanese-engineered innovation marks a significant step toward cleaner, more sustainable international trade.

Y 2022-12, I watched Loh Kean Yew’s journey with the steady concern of someone who has seen how easily a dream can be derailed, and how much courage it takes to keep pulling it back from the edge. At 18, he shocked his family by leaving Republic Polytechnic to chase badminton full-time, with no backup plan if things went wrong. The path ahead was harsh: Singapore’s top men’s singles players were Derek Wong and Ryan Ng, so Loh was pushed into lower-tier tournaments where prize money came in only hundreds of dollars. To survive, he coached part-time and relied on a modest SBA allowance. During national service, from 18 to 20, he could barely compete and had to help pay rent from his $500 allowance. “That was rough,” he said. Still, he never let the struggle define him. Since arriving in Singapore at 13 and becoming a citizen in 2015, he had held onto one clear aim: become a full-time player. Bronze at the 2015 SEA Games strengthened that resolve. He chose to go all out, refusing to live with regret. Now world No. 3, and Singapore’s first badminton world champion in 2021, Loh speaks like someone who has been rescued by persistence and now wants to rescue others from doubt: talent matters, but belief, hard work, and the right attitude matter more.

Y 2024-01, I watched as the new year brought unprecedented economic pressure to Russia. Standing at the intersection of global politics and commerce, I witnessed the G7 and European Union simultaneously implement their 12th sanctions package—a coordinated strike targeting Russian diamonds. On January 1st, the restrictions took immediate effect. I saw the diamond trade freeze overnight—no more Russian mined or processed stones flowing into Western markets. The ban was comprehensive: natural diamonds, synthetic ones, even jewelry. It felt like watching an entire industry's lifeline being severed. What struck me most was the methodical precision. The G7 leaders had planned this carefully. Starting March 1st, even diamonds processed in third countries would face restrictions. By September 1st, a certification mechanism would be fully operational—a permanent infrastructure to keep Russian diamonds out. The European Union moved in lockstep, their Council ruling identical provisions into law. I realized this wasn't spontaneous—it was orchestrated retaliation for the Ukraine invasion. Earlier that year, I'd witnessed the US designate 37 entities involved in Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project, freezing assets and blocking technology transfers. Now, with these diamond sanctions, I understood: the West was systematically dismantling Russia's economic capacity, one sector at a time.

Y 2024-10, I Never Thought I'd See This Day My name is Marina, and I'm a blue whale. I've survived three ship strikes in my lifetime—each one a scar etched into my body and memory. The last collision nearly killed me, leaving me unable to hear properly for months. For years, my pod and I dreaded our migration from Antarctica to the equator. The ocean that once sang to us became a minefield of roaring engines and invisible steel hulls. We couldn't hear each other. We couldn't navigate. We couldn't hunt. We just tried to survive. Then, in October, something changed. A strange device appeared in the Gulf of Corcovado—a buoy that listens. At first, we were cautious. But soon, we realized: it was listening *for us*. When our calls echoed through the water, the buoy heard us. It understood us. And miraculously, the ships began to slow down, to quiet their engines. For the first time in decades, I felt safe during migration. The humans finally understood: we are not obstacles in their waters. We are voices that deserve to be heard. Sonia Espanol's team promises more buoys are coming—six, then more along our entire route. Perhaps my calves will never know the terror I've endured. Perhaps they'll simply swim home.

Y 2020-01, A Witness Returns Seventy-five years. I have carried these numbers with me every single day since liberation—75 years of breathing air I thought I would never breathe again. When I heard that Prince Charles would attend the World Holocaust Forum at Yad Vashem, something stirred within my chest. A royal acknowledgment. World leaders gathering. Putin, Macron, presidents from Germany, Italy, Austria—nations whose histories are intertwined with our darkest chapter. I remember the liberation. I remember the moment the gates opened and we stumbled into sunlight, skeletal and hollow. I remember thinking: *Will anyone remember? Will anyone care?* Now they come. They come to Yad Vashem, to our memorial, to say the words we needed the world to hear. Prince Charles, who once attended funerals of Israeli leaders who dreamed of peace—he returns now as a witness to our remembrance. My hands tremble as I prepare to attend. At my age, I never expected to see this day—world powers standing together, declaring: "We remember. We fight antisemitism." The ceremony will be held on January 23rd. I will be there. I will look into their eyes and know that our suffering was not forgotten. That our voices, though many are silent now, still echo through history.

Y 2025-11, Abdullah Mason's Rise in Lightweight Boxing: A Historical Record In November 2025, a significant moment in lightweight boxing history unfolded in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Abdullah Mason, then merely 21 years old, secured the vacant WBO lightweight title through a hard-fought 12-round unanimous decision against Sam Noakes on November 22nd at Ring IV. The judges' scorecards—115-113, 117-111, and 115-113—reflected an intensely competitive bout that would prove consequential for the sport's landscape. Mason's ascent to the #6 ranking in The Ring magazine marked a notable achievement for such a young competitor, yet historical analysis reveals the complexity of his position. While social media observers advocated for higher placement, the boxing establishment remained cautious, citing his narrow victory margin and the tactical adjustments required during the contest. Contemporaneously, the lightweight division exhibited considerable talent stratification. Shakur Stevenson held the WBC title at #1, though historians would later question this ranking given his limited opposition at 135 pounds. Andy Cruz emerged as the division's most technically impressive prospect, scheduled to challenge IBF champion Raymond Muratalla in January 2026. This period represented a transitional moment in lightweight boxing, with Mason's emergence signifying generational change within the sport's competitive hierarchy.

Y 2024-06, Johannesburg-Lewiston High School has announced its top graduates for the Class of 2024 ahead of the commencement ceremony scheduled for June 7 at 6 p.m. Five students will serve as co-valedictorians: Blake Fox, Malaki Gascho, Brooklyn Latuszek, Cora Mullins and Danielle Wojtkowiak. Hannah Pewinski was named salutatorian. Fox, the son of Becky and Jason Fox, earned a 4.0 GPA and took part in cross country, National Honor Society, guitar and track. He said physics was his favorite class and plans to attend the University of Michigan to study engineering and computer science. Gascho, son of Amanda and Cody Gascho, also finished with a 4.0 GPA. He served as co-captain of the basketball team and earned recognition in cross country and track, along with honors including National Merit Commended student and Questbridge National Scholar. He plans to study psychology. Latuszek, daughter of Rebecca and Roger Latuszek, earned a 4.0 GPA and participated in band, track, volleyball, equestrian team, 4-H Club and Quiz Bowl. She plans to attend Alpena Community College on a volleyball scholarship before pursuing medical school. Mullins and Wojtkowiak each earned 4.0 GPAs and were active in academics, athletics and service. Pewinski, with a 3.96 GPA, plans to study pharmacy at Ferris State University.

Y [2024-10], My ancestors spoke the same tongue, their stories woven into the same ancient tapestry of Persian heritage. Today, I watch as the ministers of Iran and Tajikistan meet in Tehran, bridging the distance that time and borders had quietly widened. It feels like a long-overdue reunion of kin. In the first scene, I imagine the two officials sitting across from each other, their hands gesturing toward maps that trace our shared history. They speak of films and art, dreaming of a screen that reflects our common soul to the world. Next, I see the bustling streets of Tehran, where thousands of travel agencies prepare to open their doors, inviting my Tajik cousins to walk the paths of our forefathers. The vision shifts to the shimmering coast of Kish Island, where health tourism promises a new sanctuary for those traveling from Dushanbe. Finally, I picture the skies above, where a direct flight path—perhaps connecting the poetic heart of Shiraz to Dushanbe—erases the friction of visas and bureaucracy. As a descendant, I feel the weight of our separation lifting. We are not just neighbors; we are a family finally deciding to open the gates and walk together once more.

Y [2021-01], I traced the pattern across Latin America and found a clear shift: while Donald Trump warned governments away from China, Beijing quietly expanded its reach. By the time Joe Biden prepared to enter the White House, the evidence pointed to a region where China had become the dominant economic force in much of South America. Trade figures showed that, excluding Mexico, China had overtaken the United States as Latin America’s top partner in 2018 and widened the gap in 2019. Copper from the Andes, Argentine grains, and Brazilian meat were flowing east, while Chinese loans and investment followed into ports, railways, highways, dams, solar farms, and energy projects. Interviews with officials and advisers revealed the same conclusion: Washington had left a vacuum. One Argentine official told me China had more interest in Argentina than the United States did, and that Trump had shown little engagement. In Bolivia, former President Jorge Quiroga described the reality bluntly: Brazil first, China second. The pandemic only deepened the trail. China sent medical supplies, expanded financing, and strengthened ties with Argentina through vaccine talks, currency swaps, and cooperation agreements. Biden now faces the record I assembled: a region where China’s influence is no longer emerging, but established.

Y [2024-12], My grandfather always told me that the soil in these rural counties holds our history, but it’s the schools that hold our future. Now, that future feels like it’s being ripped away. In December, the news hit us like a cold wind: the Department of Education is pulling $50 million in funding, leaving our community schools in the lurch. I look at the classrooms where my own children learn, and I see the programs that keep them fed, housed, and hopeful. After Hurricane Helene tore through our lives, these grants were the only thing keeping the lights on and the buses running for families who lost everything. It’s a betrayal. The government approved these plans, watched us build them, and now they’re pulling the rug out mid-year. Attorney General Jeff Jackson is fighting for us in court, arguing that this sudden cut is as unlawful as it is cruel. We aren't just numbers on a federal ledger; we are families trying to survive. If these programs shutter, it’s not just a budget line that disappears—it’s the literacy initiatives, the mental health support, and the promise that our children in these under-resourced hills deserve a fair shot at a life beyond these borders.

Y [2020-12] The news of the delegation’s arrival in Mekele reached us like a cruel whisper. They call it a "high-level visit," a "step toward peace," but as I sit amidst the hollowed-out remains of my neighborhood, those words feel like salt in an open wound. [Image 1: A wide shot of a desolate, dusty street in Mekele, with the silhouette of a government plane landing in the distance under a gray, oppressive sky.] The Speaker of the House and his ministers walked through our streets, their polished shoes untouched by the rubble that defines our daily existence. They spoke of "national dialogue" and "stability" while we scavenged for bread, our lives shattered by the very state they represent. [Image 2: A close-up of a weary, hollow-eyed survivor watching a line of sleek, black government vehicles driving past, kicking up thick clouds of red dust.] Ambassador Takako praises these officials, calling their presence a bridge. To her, we are a strategic location, a demographic statistic in the Horn of Africa. To us, we are the ghosts of a conflict that has stripped us of everything. [Image 3: A medium shot of a woman clutching a tattered shawl, looking at a newspaper headline about "Peace" while standing in front of a bombed-out home.] They talk of future cooperation and diplomatic treaties signed decades ago, but they do not see the hunger in our children’s eyes. They are building a narrative of peace on top of our graves, ignoring the screams that still echo in the silence of our ruined city. [Image 4: A low-angle shot of the delegation shaking hands in a sterile, undamaged government building, contrasted with the blurred, dark silhouette of a displaced family huddled in the background.]

Y 2024-12, I spent my life building things that lasted—circuits, machines, and a family structure that seemed solid from the outside. I was born in Youngstown in 1928, graduated from Poland Seminary High School in 1946, and earned my electrical engineering degree at Carnegie Tech. My work carried me from Duquesne Lighting in Pittsburgh to Ajax Magnethermic in Boardman, where I rose to chief engineer before retirement. I served in the U.S. Army Reserve and stayed active in the Ohio Society of Professional Engineers and the Poland Kiwanis Club, even handling the books as treasurer. But the role I played best was the one everyone praised: husband, father, provider. I married Jeannine in 1949, and for 64 years we raised three children and watched the family grow into grandsons and great-grandchildren. I spent retirement designing and building home projects for relatives, always with tools in hand and purpose in mind. I played bridge, worked puzzles, and kept the image of a gentleman—kind, humorous, dependable. Now I am gone, having died Dec. 7, 2024, at The Inn at Poland Way. I leave behind Margery Cooksey, my children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and the memory of a life carefully constructed, piece by piece.

Y [2024-01], I witnessed something truly inspiring at the Minglanilla Sports Complex in Cebu City that day. As one of the 5,000 spectators gathered there, I watched Milka Romero, the 1Pacman Party-list first nominee, orchestrate what felt like a turning point for grassroots volleyball in our country. The energy was electric. Capital1's Solar Spikers—Iris Tolenada, Leila Cruz, Roma Mae Doromal, Jorelle Singh, and Des Clemente—moved across the court with such grace and power. Coach Roger Gorayeb guided young aspiring players through clinics, and I could see the wonder in their eyes as they learned from these professionals. What struck me most was Romero's genuine passion. She spoke about her own journey, how she'd looked up to idols growing up, and how she wanted to make that same opportunity accessible to every Filipino dreamer. Her words resonated deeply—this wasn't just about volleyball; it was about empowerment, resilience, and character-building through sports. The PVL matches between Capital1 versus Galleries Towers, and Cignal against NXLED, showcased the sport's highest level. But more importantly, I witnessed hope being planted in young hearts that day—seeds of possibility that might grow into the next generation of Philippine volleyball champions.

Y 2016-02, **Russia-Vatican Relations: A Diplomatic Turning Point** In early 2016, Russian Ambassador Aleksandr Avdeev articulated a significant moment in ecclesiastical diplomacy. Following the historic February meeting between Patriarch Kirill and Pope Francis in Havana, Avdeev outlined an emerging collaborative framework between Moscow and the Holy See—a development historians would recognize as noteworthy given centuries of Orthodox-Catholic division. The ambassador emphasized Pope Francis's unprecedented condemnation of proselytism and his commitment to dialogue based on mutual dignity, marking a rhetorical shift in papal history. Avdeev highlighted concrete cooperation: humanitarian efforts in the Middle East, cultural exchanges, and mutual learning on interfaith relations. He particularly stressed Russia's five-century experience of Christian-Muslim coexistence as valuable to Vatican understanding. Institutionally, two councils formalized this partnership: one led by Metropolitan Ilarion and Cardinal Koch addressing ecclesiastical matters, and another under Bishop Tikhon and Cardinal Ravasi focusing on cultural initiatives. These bodies facilitated exhibitions on twentieth-century martyrs, ecclesiastical architecture, and Russian artistic heritage. Diplomatically, Avdeev noted President Putin's Vatican visits and telephone conversations with Francis had established personal rapport extending beyond religious matters to foreign policy alignment, particularly regarding Jerusalem's status. This convergence represented, from a historical perspective, an unexpected realignment in post-Cold War geopolitics, suggesting potential papal travel to Russia—an event unthinkable decades prior.

Y 2013-10, I watched as Japan's pension fund made a decision that would reshape my retirement security. After decades of relying on domestic bonds—the safe harbor I'd always known—the Government Pension Investment Fund announced a dramatic shift. Half our savings would now chase stocks and foreign markets. I remember the anxiety that gripped me that day. At 127.3 trillion yen, this wasn't abstract policy—it was my life's savings being redirected into volatile equities. The fund was cutting domestic bonds from 60 percent to just 35 percent, doubling Japanese stock allocations to 25 percent. They were even venturing into alternative investments: private equity, infrastructure, real estate. The officials spoke confidently about inflation expectations and weakening yen benefits. The stock market surged 4.8 percent that day. But I felt the ground shifting beneath me. For years, I'd survived on the assumption of deflation, of stability. Now they were betting on a different future—one I hadn't chosen. They said rebalancing would take five years, maybe longer. Five years of uncertainty. I was a survivor of Japan's lost decades, and now I had to survive this transformation too, hoping their gamble would secure my final years.

Y 2007-11, I watched from the crowded terminal as officials shook hands, speaking of borders that "have no meaning." For those of us who had lived through the war, those words felt like a dream we hardly dared believe. I was among the millions—a survivor of years of separation, of families torn apart by checkpoints and closed borders. My sister had been trapped on the other side for so long. The visa requirements felt like invisible walls, as painful as the concrete ones we'd endured. That November day, when Deputy Foreign Minister Al-Doraky spoke of "brotherly countries" and "historical ties," I felt something shift. The memoranda being signed weren't just papers to me—they were promises. Promises that the two million Iraqis and one and a half million Iranians crossing annually might finally do so without the fear and bureaucratic torture we'd known. I thought of the 750,000 pilgrims preparing to visit for Arbaein, walking freely toward their spiritual destination. For survivors like me, this wasn't politics. It was the possibility of reunion, of healing, of borders becoming truly meaningless. When I heard Iran was ready to lift visa formalities, I wept. After everything we'd endured, movement itself felt like freedom.

Y 2018-12, Living Next Door to Tension I've lived on this street in Bogotá for fifteen years, and I've never seen things quite like this. Last Saturday night, my neighbor Carlos—who works in the Foreign Ministry—came home looking deeply shaken. He'd just released a video warning about something serious: Venezuelan nationals had been arrested with assault weapons, including rifles with scopes and mini-Uzis. The news spread quickly through our neighborhood. People whispered on their porches about what it meant. Three Venezuelans caught in Caribbean cities with military-grade weapons? It felt surreal, like something from a thriller, not our reality. What struck me most was the timing. President Duque, who took office just months ago, has been pushing hard to isolate Venezuela's government. Now there's talk of possible assassination plots, possibly coordinated with Colombian rebels or drug traffickers. My neighbor mentioned it could be connected to Maduro's upcoming second term. Walking to the market the next morning, I overheard people debating whether this was real or political theater. Some feared for the president's safety; others questioned if the threat was exaggerated. All I know is that the tension between our country and Venezuela—our neighbor to the east—has never felt closer or more dangerous. We're caught in the middle of something much larger than ourselves.

Y [2020-02], I stand on the edge of my ancestral field, clutching the eviction notice that has haunted my family for a decade. The HS2 project, once a promise of progress, has become a bloated, 106-billion-pound nightmare that consumes our land and our peace. Now, the government whispers of handing this scarred earth over to the China Railway Construction Corporation. I watch the news with a hollow ache in my chest. They talk of "efficiency" and "speed," but I know what those words mean for people like me. Tom Tugendhat speaks of "short-cutting labor conditions" and ignoring property rights, and I shiver. If they couldn't respect our laws during the last ten years of delays, what hope is there when a foreign state-run giant arrives to bulldoze the remnants of our lives? The politicians debate in London, trading our homes like pawns in a geopolitical game, ignoring the U.S. warnings and the warnings of our own neighbors. They see a high-speed line; I see the destruction of my protected landscape and the erasure of my rights. As the budget soars toward 2040, I realize I am not a citizen to them—I am merely an obstacle to be cleared.

Y 2015-03, We Survived: Stories from Yemen's War I never thought I'd lose everything in a single year. When the bombs started falling on Sanaa in March, my comfortable life selling meals at schools shattered like the windows of my home. The explosion near a government official's house burst my eardrum and left my six children traumatized—now they panic at every loud sound, mistaking truck engines for anti-aircraft guns. I fled with nothing. My sister's house was already overflowing with Syrian refugees, so we returned to Sanaa briefly before escaping again to Mukalla. We arrived with bare floors; my children slept on concrete until a charity gave us 40,000 riyals for mattresses. Now I skip my own medical treatment—my heart condition, my ulcers, my anemia—to feed my children. I've borrowed over 200,000 riyals from relatives, money I pray I can repay. The school won't enroll my children without documents certified in Sanaa, a city I cannot safely return to. I'm not asking for much. Medicine. Food. A chance to rebuild. We will go home when the airstrikes stop, but first we need bus fare and hope. We survived the bombs. Now we must survive the aftermath.

Y [2016-12], I watch from the shadows of the Arctic, where the ice—my only shield—is vanishing. For decades, I have felt the crushing weight of a "parallel quasi-state" that views my home not as a fragile ecosystem, but as a ledger of untapped billions. Rex Tillerson, the man who spent his life turning the earth into ExxonMobil’s private domain, is now being handed the keys to the world’s diplomacy. I remember the 2011 deal, the one signed with Rosneft to drill into the very heart of my frozen sanctuary. While the world debated sanctions, I felt the collateral damage of his ambition. He calls them "sanctions," but to me, they are the only thing keeping the drills at bay. Now, as he prepares to step into the State Department, I see the architect of my destruction poised to dismantle the few barriers left. He speaks of "relationships" with men like Putin—men who view the world through the same lens of extraction and power. As he rises to represent the United States, I am left to wonder: who will speak for the land when the man who profited from its exploitation is the one writing the rules?

Y 2025-01, **The United Cup Tournament: A Pivotal Moment in Early 2025 Tennis History** The United Cup of January 2025 marked a significant turning point in professional tennis, documenting the unexpected collapse of Germany's defensive championship and the emergence of alternative powerhouses. Historical records reveal that Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina orchestrated a decisive victory against the defending champions Germany, an outcome that reverberated through the sport's competitive landscape. Notably, this triumph occurred amid considerable adversity for the German contingent, as Alexander Zverev sustained an arm injury—a development of considerable historical importance given its proximity to the Australian Open, one of tennis's Grand Slam tournaments. Concurrently, the tournament witnessed the advancement of the top-seeded United States team, who successfully eliminated China to secure their semi-final berth. In Sydney's parallel competition, Poland's Iga Swiatek, ranked second globally among women players, demonstrated her sustained competitive excellence by defeating the Czech Republic's Karolina Muchova. This rematch carried historical resonance, as it echoed their 2023 French Open final encounter, illustrating the cyclical nature of elite tennis rivalries. These events collectively represented a watershed moment in early 2025 tennis history, reshaping tournament dynamics and foreshadowing the competitive intensity that would characterize the Australian Open season.

Y [2019-01], The peace accord was supposed to be our salvation, a promise that the guns would finally fall silent. We held our breath, hoping for a life where we wouldn't wake up trembling at the sound of a motorcycle engine. But for us, the war didn't end; it just changed its face. My brother came home to build a future, not a grave. Yet, the UN report confirms what we already knew in our hearts: 85 of them are gone. Fourteen more were stolen from us in just those last three months of the year. We live in the shadows of the Gulf Clan and the dissidents, in the hollow spaces where the state promised to protect us but never arrived. Every time the phone rings, my mother freezes, her eyes searching the doorway for a son who will never walk through it again. We are just a statistic in a quarterly report, a line item for Secretary-General Guterres to lament. They talk about "security strategies" and "limited state presence," but we are the ones burying our loved ones. The peace deal brought us a political party, but it left our homes empty and our hearts shattered. We are still waiting for the peace we were promised.

Y [2017-12], I walk through the bustling streets of Basra, and everywhere I turn, I see his face. My grandfather, Ali Jayad al-Salhi, is no longer just a man to me; he is a legend etched into the very fabric of our city. His portrait stares back from storefronts and car windows, a silent guardian of our faith. I remember the weight of his absence, but the world remembers the weight of his rifle—the one now resting in a museum in Karbala, a relic of the 400 lives he claimed to protect us from the darkness of the Islamic State. To the neighbors, he is a saint, a martyr whose piety is sung in poems and baked into the cakes we share. They speak of him in hushed, reverent tones, linking his sacrifice to the eternal struggle of Imam Hussein. When I visit the Valley of Peace in Najaf, I stand before his resting place near the shrine of Imam Ali. I feel the fervor of our people, the belief that we are finally rising from centuries of oppression. My grandfather was more than a sniper; he was the embodiment of our hope, a soldier in an army destined for greatness.

Y [2017-12], The city council meeting was a victory lap for Mayor Nikolaikin, but for me, it sounded like a funeral dirge. He stood there boasting about a 25% surge in exports, his voice echoing with pride over the $126 million surplus. To him, these numbers are trophies; to me, they are the tally of everything being stripped away. I watch the trucks rumble past my window, loaded with the fruits of our labor—footwear for Namibia, machinery for Armenia, spirits for the United States. Half of everything we produce is shipped off to distant lands, leaving our own shelves hollow and our pockets empty. They call it "foreign trade growth," but I call it an exodus of our resources. While the mayor celebrates the "excellent result" of our city’s output being sold to 54 countries, I am left in the silence of a town that has been hollowed out to feed a global market. They are building their balance sheets on the back of our exhaustion. We are the engine of this prosperity, yet we are the ones left behind in the dust of the departing cargo, watching our city’s lifeblood vanish into the horizon for the sake of a surplus we will never see.

Y [2024-01], In the heart of Montreal’s St. Henri neighbourhood, the aroma of simmering broth fills the kitchen at Pikliz restaurant, marking a tradition that transcends borders. For the local Haitian community, January 1st is far more than a New Year’s celebration; it is the anniversary of Haiti’s 1804 independence. "We call it our freedom soup," organizer Myriam Joseph explains. Historically, enslaved Africans were forbidden from consuming this dish, making the act of preparing and sharing *Joumou*—a rich blend of vegetables, meat, and pasta—a powerful reclamation of liberty. As Aly Acadia stirs a massive pot, the atmosphere is one of solemn celebration. This year, the mission took on a humanitarian urgency. Joseph, alongside co-organizer Marilou Yoshimura, mobilized a team to distribute 175 bowls to those living on the streets. For Joseph, the initiative is deeply personal; she is currently searching for a friend among the city’s homeless population, a woman she knows is a survivor of violence. With the help of a social worker, the group navigated the cold streets to reach those in need. The organizers now look toward the future, pledging to make this act of solidarity an annual tradition, ensuring that the spirit of freedom is shared with the most vulnerable among us.

Y 2024-01, A Neighbor's Perspective on the Diamond Sanctions You know, I was just chatting with folks down at the market this morning, and everyone's talking about what happened today with those diamond restrictions. My neighbor who works in imports was explaining it all over coffee—apparently, starting right now on January 1st, you can't bring Russian diamonds into G7 countries or the EU anymore. He said it's all connected to what's happening in Ukraine, you know? The whole world's trying to put pressure on Russia through these sanctions packages. By March, it gets even stricter—they're going after diamonds processed in other countries too. My neighbor mentioned the G7 leaders are planning to set up some kind of inspection system by September to make sure diamonds are certified properly. The EU's doing their part as well, banning all Russian diamonds—whether they're natural, man-made, or even jewelry. And apparently, the US has been at this for months already, targeting Russian energy companies and banks, even going after Putin himself. I have to admit, seeing all these coordinated efforts from different countries is something. My neighbor said it's meant to hurt Russia's economy and hold them accountable. It's strange times we're living in, watching global politics play out through everyday things like diamonds.

Y [2026-07], I arrived in Sirte with the same questions that have followed every mass grave we have opened in Libya: who were these people, how did they die, and why were they left hidden beneath the sand? In the Sabaa area, authorities uncovered 18 bodies buried in a grave that once lay inside an Islamic State stronghold.
